subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF APPOINTMENT OF JAMES JOHNSON MACDONELL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the pleasure to announce to the House the appointment by the Governor in Council of Mr. James Johnson Macdonell as Auditor General of Canada, effective July 1, 1973.
Mr. G. R. Long, the present assistant Auditor General, has been appointed as acting Auditor General effective March 25.

Mr. Macdonell will be replacing Mr. Maxwell Henderson who, after 13 years of loyal service reaches on March 24 the compulsory retirement age laid down by the Financial Administration Act.

Wishing to secure the services of an outstanding member of the accounting profession, the government asked senior partners of accounting firms across the country to suggest the names of persons who would be suitable for appointment as Auditor General.
Mr. Macdonell was one of those who were thus highly recommended and I know that he will fulfil his duties with the required skill and competence.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will reply very briefly to the very interesting statement by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) simply by saying that I hope the newly appointed Auditor General will be as effective, independent and objective as the previous Auditor General.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF APPOINTMENT OF JAMES JOHNSON MACDONELL
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF APPOINTMENT OF JAMES JOHNSON MACDONELL
speechtext: We trust that in the exercise of his duties he will continue to put the fear of the Lord into this government. When the government changes, in the unlikely event that we do anything that we should not we hope he will do the same to us.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF APPOINTMENT OF JAMES JOHNSON MACDONELL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we welcome the unusually swift action of the government in dealing with this matter. We are pleased to note the method that the government has used in securing the name of a person for recommendation to this important post. We wish Mr. Macdonell well in the performance
of his duties as a servant of this parliament. I am also happy to echo the sentiments expressed by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin). We hope that the new Auditor General will indeed put the fear of the Lord into whatever government sits to Your Honour's right.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF APPOINTMENT OF JAMES JOHNSON MACDONELL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think this is a good opportunity to thank Mr. Henderson for his services to this country. A number of us have had occasion to appreciate his many contributions of evidence to the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
We are confident that his successor will give the same degree of satisfaction to hon. members, both in committee and in his annual reports. We also hope that the new Auditor General will not have cause to complain of a lack of staff to help him fulfil his duties. It is all very well to pick competent people for important jobs, but the checking of public accounts also requires the training of competent personnel in sufficient numbers to enable the Auditor General to do his job properly.
We therefore trust that the new Auditor General, whose competence we do not question, will have at his disposal adequate staff and funds to enable him to carry out his task efficiently.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING NEIGHBOURHOOD IMPROVEMENT, REHABILITATION, OWNERSHIP, NEW COMMUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to continue my remarks from yesterday. If Toronto contractors say that an oversupply of serviced lots would be created by implementation of the just mentioned measure, this would soon bring the price of a normal lot to half the present $40,000 plus average. Prices could be reduced even more, to say $5,000, if developers were committed to building single family homes on smaller lots with a minimum of services; a good gravel road, open storm sewers and overhead power lines. By eliminating the sales taxes and in some cases substituting cheaper materials such as aluminum siding for brick veneer, the cost of a house, now about $18,000 to $20,000 for a three bedroom bungalow, in most urban areas, could be reduced to about $15,000. These are the views of the developers and all levels of government should listen to them. What is even more important though, is that the federal government listen to the demands of the provinces in relation to housing.
The $1.5 million study launched recently by the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) to discover regional housing needs in Canada is a waste of the taxpayers money. Obviously, various regions in Canada have different problems. All this study will tell us is what we already know. In addition, how is parliament to be subjected to government housing studies? My hon. colleague, the former minister responsible for housing, submitted his task force report on housing in January, 1969. Now, after four years, the government is spending $1.5 million to discover that in this country separate approaches are required in dealing with different regional housing needs. This government refuses to accept the fact that the provinces know more about regional housing needs because, together with municipal governments, they have been building houses and controlling housing. Constitutionally as well, land use and housing are within provincial jurisdiction. But the government refuses to listen to the provinces. Several provinces want the federal government to get out of the housing field and let them take over housing programs if they can be granted the tax revenues to pay for them. The federal government, though, refuses to

yield. The block financing, which the provinces temporarily accepted and by which the government will hand over all moneys allotted for housing, will allow the provinces to decide how to best spend the money.
Hopefully, the provinces and municipalities will see fit to begin assembling land. The best way to enable a low-income person to become a homeowner may be to take the actual cost of land out of the purchase figure. Cities could begin land banking. They should acquire land for residential development and retain ownership on it. Houses should be built on these lands, and then sold. The land, however, should not be sold. A policy such as this would enable the poor to have a home. It would also prevent the land speculation that keeps pushing up the cost of houses. All this though would be a start, but the federal government must heed not only the advice of the developers but also that of the provincial governments. While it is the job of the provincial government to produce housing stock that people can afford, it is the job of the federal government to give them the power to do so.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, with respect to costs, may I say that the monster inflation has got completely out of hand, especially in the area of housing. Here again, figures can be deceptive. A house which was priced at $16,000 in 1960 and today costs $24,000 is not just 50 per cent higher, but in the end turns out to be more like 150 per cent higher because of interest and other charges. By rough rule of thumb, an increase of one per cent in the interest rate adds 10 per cent to the capital cost of shelter, so that the 4 per cent increase in mortgage rates from the early 1960's added a hefty 40 per cent to the consumers' long-term bill for housing. The cost of buying the average NHA house actually doubled in the 1965-1970 period. Back in 1960, about half of Canadian families could afford to buy the average NHA house; now the percentage is more like 10 per cent and in the Toronto area it is closer to 5 per cent. The availability of single family homes for Canadians has almost become extinct. The minister's bill provides too little too late.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING NEIGHBOURHOOD IMPROVEMENT, REHABILITATION, OWNERSHIP, NEW COMMUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one would have thought that because of our rigorous climate and the amount of investment involved in housing, politicians in Canada would have tended to escape any obligation to deal with that topic. I am sure hon. members on both sides of this House will agree that Canada's record in respect of housing should be the envy of many nations throughout the world. I would suggest that the difficulties faced by previous generations with regard to housing deserve a great deal of our national attention. One need only be reminded of the sod shanties of the great northwest as well as the log cabins of northern Ontario to realize what tremendous strides we have achieved in relation to housing. There is no doubt that the proposals before us do not offer a complete solution to this particular problem. There are still a number of strides to be made. To indicate that the provisions of the act or the amendments proposed would all prove to be beyond reproach would indeed be to engage in day dreaming in colour panavision.
However, I challenge any member of this House to suggest any previous bills with which this House has had the pleasure of dealing which have contained such imaginative provisions and which have exhibited such
March 22, 1973

serious and concentrated thought. I do not propose to deal with all aspects of the new amendments. I shall content myself with stressing three major aspects. The first is that of co-operative housing and the non-profit association involvement. The second provision with which I propose to deal is that in respect of loans to be made to individuals to facilitate ownership. The third very important topic, to my mind, involves the provisions relating to new communities.
Since World War II, Canada has indeed been favoured by a multiplicity of volunteer organizations which have been engaged, supported by private funds, in assisting individual groups of citizens requiring specialized assistance. This legislation has been inspired by the success of these voluntary associations. The legislation thus inspired is a recognition of the success achieved by these non-profit organizations in the past in providing needed accommodation of good quality. The loans which will be made available to these associations will be in amounts of up to 100 per cent of the lending value of the project with amortization over a period of 50 years. Further, these voluntary organizations will have the advantage of a $10,000 fund which could be employed in planning and preparing their own projects for completion.

The bill before us also provides for similar aid to some co-operatives that wish to build, purchase or improve houses and then sell them to their members or to others that are interested in supplying particular groups, most of which are members, with new or repaired housing they have acquired.
The provisions under clause 34 of the bill entitle them to a low rate of interest, a 40-year mortgage, and to a contribution by the CMHC to payment of the capital, interest and taxes.
We will thus have the authority of a statutory regulation to give the underprivileged assistance in paying the principal and the interest, in addition to which they will have access to public funds when paying municipal taxes.
Mr. Speaker, this legislation also goes to show that this government is inclined towards greater social justice and to giving priority to those with small incomes whose needs are greatest.
Moreover, the second class of co-operatives, those that will be renting accommodation, will be providing homes for those who really need them, through non-profit organizations which try to promote greater social justice for this country. Co-operatives formed with that precise purpose in mind will also be eligible for 10,000-dollar subsidies to help with the planning and execution of their projects. The co-operative associations will obtain up to 100 per cent of the loan value of the project. Public funds will be available to them to meet their immediate commitments, that is the payment of interest or municipal taxes.
This brings me to my second point. We saw, when dealing with co-operatives, that these particular projects make it possible for individual citizens without the necessary income to buy their own houses in accordance with the
National Housing Act
state of the market. The added benefit of this provision is that public funds can be obtained in order to achieve the same purpose. The National Housing Act as amended does indeed provide for assistance to individuals who are unable to buy their own house. They will be provided with a mortgage through CMHC at a low interest rate, lower than the one which exists in the market. They will also be provided with terms of up to 40 years for amortization, and furthermore, they will be provided with public funds, administered under the regulations, in order to help them meet those payments which as a family unit, they might otherwise not be able to meet.
There are but a few pages to this bill. It may not offer solutions to all the problems but, I suggest, it offers solutions to a considerable degree. I suggest that they are directly in accordance with the principles of social justice that have been advocated, not only by this government but generally by all Canadians whatever their political persuasion might be, because we have attempted to provide low rental housing for individuals with low incomes. We have seen governments interfering with the rights of individuals. We have seen governments erecting the buildings, renting them and administering them, and it has frequently been the experience that individuals residing in those particular buildings have not been of primary importance to the administrator.
I suggest to hon. members that under this bill we will be able to reinstate the individual to the important position which he held. The individual will build his home or arrange for its construction, and then he will be able to obtain the necessary financing. If he is not in receipt of a sufficient income to enable him to provide for himself and his family and to meet all the obligations of the contract that he has undertaken, public funds will be made available to him, not as a charity but on a properly administered basis. I would suggest further that the bill recognizes the necessity for people to exercise initiative and it rejects the concept of paternalism. It foresees the complete integration of low income families into our comfortable middle class neighbourhoods without any aspersions being cast on their participation.
As an example of the wisdom of the particular provisions, I will cite a particularly appropriate case. A group of senior citizens can make an application under the provisions of the act to obtain funding to prepare a plan or project. Having prepared and submitted their plan, they can make an application for the financing of that project. They can then ensure the proper execution of those plans, and upon the completion of the project they can benefit from the fruits of their own creation and have the satisfaction of knowing that in the future others with the same needs will be able to reap the same benefits.
The Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) is to be congratulated for his foresight and inventiveness with reference to the provisions in the bill. Yet, to my mind there are other provisions which are even more startling, and I hope that they are only an indication of things to come. For the first time we have in the House a recognition of the concept of whole community planning, not partial but whole community planning. A fund of $100 million will be set aside and made available, and in conjunction with the provinces, which nevertheless exercise
March 22, 1973

National Housing Act
primary jurisdiction with reference to municipal affairs, it can be employed to plan and to erect communities. That is not a brand new idea, although it is the first time it has been introduced in the House. Indeed, an experiment is being conducted in Minnesota in the United States where complete urban is being undertaken from first principles.
I must call the attention of hon. members to a long standing experiment in the U.S.S.R. Until recently, we did not consider the experiences of that country with such a different philosophy to be of much assistance. However, I was guided to a book by Farley Mowat published in 1970 entitled "Sibir" which deals with Siberia and two trips which the Canadian author has taken into that area. Throughout the book he indicates his amazement at the use that has been made of Siberia, a corner of the earth which has not always received a warm reception in our conversations. I should like to quote from pages 26 and 27 of this book. Prior to this quotation he writes of the development of Siberia and the municipalities in that area, and he goes on to say:
Between Sverdlovsk and the halfway mark at Irkutsk, there's a string of big cities four or five hundred miles apart. Most of them began in the seventeenth century as forts, trading stations and administrative centres and until the 1930's they were backwoods towns with wooden buildings and mud streets. Most of Siberia was one big backwater in those days. Then in the mid 1930's it began to be obvious what Hitler had in mind and our leaders could see there was a good chance much of European Russia might be overrun. If that happened the Urals were going to serve as our last line of defence.
The government began moving whole factory towns-machines and people-from Western Russia across the Urals. By the time the war ended provincial places like Sverdlovsk and Omsk had turned into industrial cities, and after the war they kept on growing, faster and faster. Siberia came awake with a jump! Within fifteen years the whole western region of the Trans Sib, as far east as Irkutsk, had jumped into modern times. Sverdlovsk, Omsk, Novosibirsk, Krasnoyarsk, Bratsk, Irkutsk, the flame of a new industrial society set each one of them alight in turn. They've got almost four million people between them now, and they'll have double that by 1975 . ..
What does all this have to do with the speech that I am giving, you may ask? I am suggesting that, with the very modest attempt being made now by the Secretary of State for Urban Affairs, we are seeing the concept to city planning in much the same manner as it has occurred in other places. As a northerner who has always advocated greater dispersal of our population into those areas which are apt to be developed in the future by someone else other than ourselves if we do not take the initiative, I welcome the provisions in this particular statute. I think that in the very near future we will see a greater development of this concept.
When I talk about city planning, I do not seek to encourage the concept of satellites to metro Toronto. I am thinking of communities set in virgin lands, where they will become viable. Of course, everything we are dealing with today, such as energy policy, economic policy, cultural policy, is attached to the development of our society. One of the basic concerns now is to try to analyse where we are going, and I suggest that the minister ought to be congratulated for having given us the opportunity to do so.
I wish to indicate that I am going to vote for this bill because I think it is a most worthwhile one. I am sure all hon. members would agree that it should be passed without any dissension because hon. members, in conscience, should ensure that their constituents are made aware of all the benificial aspects of this bill so that they will be able to derive the maximum advantage from it. I take it, Mr. Speaker, that the purpose of these debates is to analyse all these provisions to that end, to benefit from them at the time the bill is approved, which I again suggest should be without undue delay.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING NEIGHBOURHOOD IMPROVEMENT, REHABILITATION, OWNERSHIP, NEW COMMUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my contribution to this debate I propose not to focus on specific details of the bill before us, but rather to speak about general principles.
I am going to argue that federal housing policies, current or proposed, do more harm than good, and that the best thing the federal government could do to help us Canadians with our housing problems would be to leave us alone. Disband the bureaucracies, cut taxes, and let us solve our own problems, with the interference of our local or provincial governments if we choose, but without federal interference, without federal bureaucrats taking our money from us in taxes and spending it as they want it spent rather than as we want it spent.
In some cases local or provincial governments may foolishly pursue policies which, I would argue, do more harm than good. But if a local or provincial government pursues an unsound policy it clearly does less damage than is done by the federal government's pursuing that same policy. Furthermore, as it is most unlikely that all provincial governments would simultaneously pursue the same unsound policy, unless all provinces were to simultaneously suffer Liberal or NDP governments, divergencies in provincial policies would give Canadians the opportunity to study the effects of different policies pursued simultaneously in the various provinces, an opportunity which the federal government denies when it imposes a uniform policy on all of Canada.
The mayor of my city, Vancouver, Art Phillips, has written of:
"One basic principle .. . That principle is that government should be as close to the people as possible. In Canada, that means that government should be as decentralized as possible."
I agree with him.
Another basic principle that I would like to talk about is the principle that no one can ever say what would make anyone else happy. No one is in any position to tell me that if I were to spend more of my time or money on some things rather than on other things, I would be happier than I am now. All of our individual preferences are purely subjective. There are no such things as objective standards or preferences which will make a human being happy. For any given preference held by you or me, someone prefers the opposite. For example, some people prefer carrots to spinach, while others prefer spinach to carrots. Consider a more extreme example. Although I attach very great value to sustaining my own life, there are people who prefer the opposite: suicide. Their subjective preferences are such that they are happier to choose death than to choose life.

March 22, 1973

Even more highly than my life, I value my liberty. Other people care little about their liberty, and history shows that such people usually lose their liberty. Some people, fortunately a minority, are pleased that over the last century the state has been progressively consuming our liberty, taking us back toward the serfdom of the dark ages, "turning back the clock", so to speak. I am not pleased with this loss of liberty. In a free society we respect each other's subjective preferences, and we ask of each other merely that each refrain from forcibly imposing his preferences on others, either directly or through the state's power of legal coercion.
You may ask, what does all this have to do with housing? Simply this: There are some people who have some idea of what sort of housing they like. They call their choice of housing "decent" housing. Then, they want to use the power of the federal government to coerce, directly or indirectly, all the people into living in such housing.
If I prefer to spend some of my money on what they call "sub-standard" housing and the rest of my money on other things, then they want to take my money from me in taxes, and spend it on so-called "urban renewal", tearing down my house and building a concrete ghetto for me to live in. I wish they would leave me alone, and stop taxing me and pushing me around. They cannot prove that their way of life is in any objective way any better than mine. Why, then, should they be able, in a supposedly free country, to use the power of the state to force their personal preferences on me? I am quite willing to leave them alone.
It may be argued that some people are so poor that they cannot afford housing more attractive-in our opinion- than the housing they presently occupy, and that the government should build so-called "decent" housing for these people. For the time being let us leave aside a discussion of the ways in which modern governments impoverish people-for example, compulsory mis-educa-tion, oppressive taxation, denial of the right to work, and exorbitant tariffs, especially on things like shoes and shirts-in order that we may focus on the distinction between the question of poverty and the question of housing.
If a particular poor person were very much richer he still might not want to change his housing. He may prefer to do other things with his additional wealth or income rather than buy more expensive housing. But whatever he does with his additional wealth, he does precisely that because that gives him more satisfaction than he would derive from any alternative course of action. Some people enjoy hoarding money. I am sure many hon. members have heard of apparently impoverished people who have died, leaving $50,000 or more tucked in a mattress. Many wealthy people choose to live quite modestly. You or I might spend the money differently-if it were ours to spend-in accordance with our respective preferences, but our preferences are not theirs.
If it is really our desire to raise the material standard of living of poor people, rather than push them around and run their lives, then we should abandon the government policies that impoverish them. In place of the present mess of welfare schemes and housing schemes, we should
National Housing Act
give the poor people the cash presently spent on these things and let the poor people spend the cash in the ways that give them the greatest satisfaction. To build our preferred type of housing for the poor people and to hire thousands of bureaucrats to oversee them in these ghettos is wasteful. The amount of waste is the amount of satisfaction the poor people would gain if they could spend the money themselves on what they consider to be their most urgent needs, over and above the amount of satisfaction, if any, they get from living in the poor people's ghettos that we have been building for them.
Some people say that the price of land is too high and that the federal government should adopt certain measures, such as land banking, to lower the price of land. I will argue shortly that although lower land prices may be considered a desirable end, land banking is not a means that will in reality achieve that end. Instead, land banking will raise the price of land.
The market price of land is determined by supply and demand; this is a fact of nature which government cannot change. If government were to impose legal controls on the price of land, it still could not change the market price, the price at which the seller is willing to sell and the buyer is willing to buy. If government decrees that a certain piece of land shall not legally sell for more than $10,000, if the owner is not willing to sell for less than $12,000 and if there is a buyer willing to pay $12,000, then the government's law cannot change the reality that the market price is $12,000. To please the government, the buyer and seller may state on a piece of paper that the exchange price was $10,000, and pass $2,000 under the table. But the government's laws cannot change the reality of the market price. The government's laws may drive discussion of market price out of the legal market place and into the free market, sometimes called the "black market", but the government's laws cannot change the realities of the market. For example, rent controls in New York City failed to control actual rents, the difference between the real rent and the legal rent being passed under the table as "key money".
Through expropriation, government may seize land from some people, paying them less than fair market price, and resell the land to its friends at the expropriation price. But here government has no more lowered the market price of land than a bank robber lowers the market interest rate on loans.
Prices of land are higher now than they have been in years. The main reason for the increases in land prices is the paper money inflation that the federal government has been causing through the Bank of Canada. For years the federal government has been behaving in a way that would have put a private company into bankruptcy long ago: its spending has far exceeded its revenues. It has been unwilling to behave responsibly, to do what is unpleasant, to impose taxes high enough to meet its expenditures or, alternatively, to reduce its expenditures. Instead, hoping in the short run to win popularity with the voters, the government has been doing what no private company can do: it has been using the Bank of Canada to issue paper money to cover its deficits.
But now the unruly economic chickens have come home to roost. All that new paper money has caused a terrible

March 22, 1973
National Housing Act
inflation. Like all the other governments that have caused paper money inflations over the past 200 years, this government has tried to blame the inflation on supposedly greedy tradesmen, merchants, and landowners. But we are not fooled! We know that the tradesmen, merchants, and landowners are no more or less greedy than they have been at any other time in history, during inflation or deflation. Human nature stays pretty much the same. We know that the price that a man demands for his labour, goods, or land is not going to be the price he actually gets, unless money is available to pay that price. And the greater the supply of money available, the higher the prices that people demand. And who controls the money supply? Tradesmen? Merchants? Landowners? No, the federal government controls the money supply, through the Bank of Canada.
During periods of inflation increases in land prices usually exceed increases in other prices. It is easy to see why. Even though the federal government preaches much nonsense about inflation, my constituents, especially those who have lived through paper money inflations in other countries, know that even though the government can print money, the government cannot print land. So, to protect their savings from the government's inflation, they buy land. Thus, they want to buy more land than they would want to buy in the absence of the paper money inflation. And so the demand for land is increased disproportionately, and this demand pushes prices up disproportionately. What is the remedy to the problem of rapidly rising land prices? Stop the paper money inflation.
A long time ago the economist Henry George pointed out that the supply of land is fixed by nature; the supply of land cannot be increased. Therefore, the price of land is determined by demand. How can government land banking possibly reduce the price of land? If government goes out to buy land, it increases the total demand for land. To everyone else's demand for land is added government's demand for land. Unless the government plans to use expropriation to selectively seize particular pieces of land from particular people, it can buy land only by out-bidding other buyers, that is to say, driving up the price.
Not only will government land banking not do any good, it will do a great deal of harm. It will drive up land prices. It will be a terrible invitation to corruption; politicians and bureaucrats will be tempted to use the taxpayers' money to overpay for land bought from their friends and will be tempted to sell the so-called "banked" land to other friends at prices below fair market price. And it would give politicians and bureaucrats an increased opportunity to injure their enemies through expropriation.
We would do well to note that when government engages in the selective seizure of land through expropriation, paying less than fair market price, it is not the big corporation but rather the little man, often the small farmer, who suffers most. The little man cannot afford to fight back effectively; he cannot afford to hire the best lawyers; he cannot afford to spend time and money on appeals. And the government knows it. The government knows that in expropriation proceedings it has the little

man at its mercy, and rarely does the government extend him any mercy.
An observation about the effect of the government's paper money inflation on interest rates is relevant. The observation is very simple: inflation of the supply of paper money causes interest rates to rise. Let me illustrate this point with an example. Suppose that in the absence of inflation the market rate of interest is 3 per cent, because 3 per cent is the price at which the amount of money that people are willing to lend equals the amount which people are willing to borrow. For instance, in 1936 the government was able to sell its issue of 3 per cent perpetual bonds to investors who believed in the stability of the dollar. Suppose the government inflates the money supply at a rate which causes price inflation to reach a rate of 5 per cent per year. On the lending side, people will want at least 8 per cent on their money-in order to get their 3 per cent interest plus 5 per cent compensation for inflation. On the borrowing side, people who in the absence of inflation would be willing to pay only 3 per cent are now on the whole willing to pay 8 per cent, which is the original 3 per cent plus the 5 per cent inflation premium. They are willing to pay this amount because they expect that the prices of the goods, labour, or land that they sell will rise with the general inflation. The remedy to high interest rates is the same as the remedy to high and rising land prices: Stop the paper money inflation.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, I have spoken about several things: the need for decentralization of government; the wastefulness of government's spending money to buy things like housing for people rather than letting the people spend the money themselves in the ways that give them, not government bureaucrats, the greatest satisfaction. I have spoken about the foolishness of government land banking, the futility of government attempts to fix market prices and, finally, of the great evil that lies at the root of high land prices and high interest rates, the government's paper money inflation.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I have tried to explain that government is not the solution of our problems.

Government is the problem, especially this government. When we recognize that basic fact, when we recognize that, as Bastiat said over a century ago, the state is the great fiction by which everyone tries to live at the expense of everyone else; when we recognize that government, which is simply the power of legal coercion, can destroy but not create, can build nothing of itself but can seize only what others have created; when we recognize that it is folly to think that government can solve our problems for us, when the only resources at the government's disposal are our resources; when we recognize that asking the government to solve our problems will simply result in government's telling us how to live our lives, and enforcing its instructions with its police power; only then, Mr. Speaker, will we have a truly free and prosperous society.
March 22, 1973

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING NEIGHBOURHOOD IMPROVEMENT, REHABILITATION, OWNERSHIP, NEW COMMUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with very great pleasure that I rise to talk about the amendments to the National Housing Act.
I endorse the efforts of the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) of which I am very satisfied. His interventions are very timely since urban concerns are more and more important.
Mr. Speaker, I represent an urban riding of downtown Toronto. I am an old Torontonian of the fourth or fifth generation. I can say proudly, Mr. Speaker, that my family has been living in downtown Toronto for more that one and a half century.
I am very much aware of the problems of that large Canadian city and I am convinced that the minister's efforts will help solve not only today's complex problems but those of the future of urban living in Canada as well. [English]
I listened to the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke) with great interest. I was informed, after listening to the hon. gentleman, that possibly we had better all go home, because there is not room for government at all, if I understood him correctly.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING NEIGHBOURHOOD IMPROVEMENT, REHABILITATION, OWNERSHIP, NEW COMMUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext: There is no room for this government.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING NEIGHBOURHOOD IMPROVEMENT, REHABILITATION, OWNERSHIP, NEW COMMUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I compliment the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) for his positive attitude on these amendments to the National Housing Act. This is an enlightened measure and is an alternative to the bulldozer approach, and therefore especially deserving of support. I particularly direct your attention, Sir, to clause 27, to that part called the neighbourhood improvement plan. This is of great importance to areas of downtown Toronto. I believe the most refreshing part is that found in clause 27.1(2)(c). I can imagine the confused consternation of my friends opposite when they learned that the federal government intended to introduce consultation among neighbours who are involved in each urban improvement project.
In the area I represent, Sir, participation has taken on an important aspect. In my riding, Spadina, there is at the moment a conflict over a block called the hydro block. This is an area that was taken over by Ontario Hydro and, because of protests from local residents, the Ontario Housing Corporation took over the block and asked the residents what they would like to have done with it. The residents formed a committee and made exhaustive studies in terms of the physical, social and economic value of the block. They came up with 14 points, most of them reasonable. The provincial minister in charge of Ontario Housing Corporation has yet to respond in a positive way to the neighbours. It is with pleasure that I note the minister has introduced this form of consultation in these amendments to the National Housing Act.
Another important aspect relating to the neighbourhood improvement plan is to be found in other parts of clause 27. There are many excellent implications to this amendment, those involving open space, for example. The federal government will be making a 50 per cent contribution in this regard. The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) pointed out the other day that here we have poten-
National Housing Act
tial funding for day-care centres, so important in our urban areas and so neglected by many provincial governments. Also, under this part of the bill there is room for the establishment of neighbourhood recreation centres.
We have heard, during the past few days, members on the other side of the House speaking of their interest in the decaying centre cores of cities. I really wonder if any of those members have ever been in the downtown area of a city, or if their view has been that obtained from a limousine as it proceeded from Bay Street out of town to the country club. Apparently they have no understanding or conception of what it is like to live in the downtown area of a modern Canadian city.
I have heard concern expressed about building maintenance standards. I suggest to you, Sir, that if the city of Toronto building inspectors applied strictly the building bylaws in the riding of Spadina, the aldermen would be in great difficulty. The proponents of capital punishment would have a field day as they hanged the aldermen from city hall. The bylaws are not strictly applied in the city of Toronto. Anyone who knows the area knows that nobody would be crazy enough to apply building bylaws strictly in the downtown area. One of the reasons for the healthiness of downtown Toronto-and contrary to some statements downtown Toronto is certainly not in a state of urban decay-and one of the reasons the city has become famous in this regard has to do with immigrants. In my riding there are people who speak 33 different languages. Over the past 20 years, they have completed probably the largest urban renewal project in the world. We have street after street of sparkling houses; they are old houses made new, privately, without any government help. The only assistance has been from understanding building inspectors. There were probably 2,000 illegal toilets in Toronto. Cellars have been made over. Attics have been fixed up. Extra families have moved in to help with the expense of renovation. It goes on and on and this, I emphasize, should be encouraged. Toronto building inspectors generally apply bylaws sensibly.
All the same, Mr. Speaker, there must be minimum standards, particularly when you deal with conscienceless landlords, of which we have many. The only defence many people in this country have against living in unheated shacks, without windows and with cracks in the ceilings is minimum standards. The areas of northern Ontario where people live in very cold shacks are areas for which no minimum standards are prescribed. This is an important part of the bill before us.
I believe, too, that the neighbourhood improvement program has great implications for the future. Hon. members may recall that in Britain after the war a system of trust houses was established to preserve so-called stately homes. Such a program has application in cities like Toronto where, because of population pressure, land in the downtown area has become expensive. I am thinking, in particular, of an area in Toronto known as The Annex. My great-grandfather was a small contractor who built many solid houses in that neighbourhood. For the benefit of those who do not know Toronto very well, I might say that The Annexe is an area around Avenue Road and Bloor; it was incorporated into the City of

March 22, 1973
National Housing Act
Toronto about 1900. In the 'seventies it was an area of market gardeners. Members of my family still live there in a house built by my great-grandfather in the 'eighties. Land there now has tremendous value. I know of a case where a house with a 25-foot frontage and no great depth sold five years ago for $86,000.
I suggest that the program called the trust system could be applied to downtown areas such as The Annex. These are gracious streets. They contribute to the urban life of those who are obliged through economic circumstances to live in our cities. They are areas which should not be destroyed. Yet who can really say it is wise on economic grounds to continue to live in a house, a modest house when built, a nine-roomed house, which today has a market value of $100,000? There is no economic justification for it. The reason can only be that it contributes to the wellbeing of the citizens generally. So I see in the neighbourhood improvement plan the possibility of freezing some of these areas and preserving some of the amenities for the sake of the wellbeing of the citizens in general. I hope we may come to accept the concept of people living in a house in trust, a house owned, really, by the community as a whole. Whether we like it or not, I believe we are moving in this direction toward the establishment of what I call trust neighbourhoods.
The bill we are considering is not an answer to all the housing needs of Canadians. I agree with the submission of the Metro-Toronto Housing Task Force that the amount of forgiveable loan toward the rehabilitation of older housing stock should be increased from $2,000 to $4,000 in the case of low income families. I am concerned that middle-income groups, professional people, may move into too many improved houses downtown, thereby reducing the number of houses available to lower income groups whose possibility of movement is far less than those with higher incomes.
Some of the hyperbole emanating from the other side of this chamber in the past few days has really been fantastic. If I did not know better I would say it came from people who were engaged in the land speculating business. Last Thursday, the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) used excruciatingly exaggerated figures about the cost of a house in Toronto. He said the cheapest house one could buy today cost $35,000. Where did he get that figure? He says he got it from the Urban Development Institute. This, I think, is indicative. The Urban Development Institute is an association of apartment builders who have direct financial interest in overstating the price of the average house because it is in their interest to demolish houses and build apartments. The Metro-Toronto Task force and the Social Planning council list the price of a house in Toronto at $25,000, $10,000 less than the figure quoted by the hon. member for Calgary North.
After giving us the figure provided to him by people in the apartment construction business, the hon. member proceeded to tell us that every Canadian was "entitled to a home with a landscape." I wonder what kind of landscape he would get from the twentieth floor of an apartment building. I would call it an airscape, certainly not a landscape. The phrase reminded me of a speech I have read- was it made in Louisana?-promising "a chicken in every

pot". The average Canadian will not buy that kind of nonsense.
I take pleasure in associating myself with the minister in supporting the bill, and in associating myself with the brief that was presented by the Metro Toronto Housing Task Force. The brief states that Bill C-133 indicates a new direction for housing policy in this country. Incidentally, this task force was comprised of a group of 100 people specializing in housing needs in densely populated urban areas. The brief goes on to state that the task force "welcomes these initiatives and considers them a forward step in the provision of adequate housing for all Canadians".

speakeroldname: Mr. Walter C. Carter (St. John's West):
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING NEIGHBOURHOOD IMPROVEMENT, REHABILITATION, OWNERSHIP, NEW COMMUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is rather amusing to sit in this House and listen to members on the other side pretending to be interested in the housing problems we face in Canada. It is these same people who allowed this situation to develop, refusing to take any concrete action to deal with the various recommendations and reports made to the government during the last five years I have been in this House. These same people are now talking about the need for new housing legislation and decrying the problem being experienced by people of low and middle income. They are pretending to be concerned and to take an interest in what is happening.
I was amused to hear the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Stollery) talk a moment ago of the need for more and better housing in his riding. He took issue with the statement of my colleague, the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams), concerning the average cost of a house in Toronto. The hon. member opposite stated that rather than $35,000 being the average price, $25,000 would be a more realistic figure. It seems to me that the hon. member must have his wires crossed, because I am getting signals back, and have been for some time, that to buy a building lot in Toronto would probably set one back as much as $18,000 or more. So I am at a loss to understand where the hon. member gets his figure of $25,000 as being the average cost of a house in Toronto. Indeed, in my own city of St. John's, Newfoundland, this figure would be considered to be very low. I do not have the exact figure here, but I would be willing to bet that the average cost of a home in St. John's, Newfoundland, would exceed the amount of money mentioned by the hon. member for Spadina.
In rising to speak on this bill, I should like to say I have certain reservations about it. The last time that this legislation came before the House, the government called an election before it had a chance of being passed. In speaking on this bill today, I am wondering whether the government will pull the rug out from under my feet, or whether the walls of the building will collapse, or, better still, perhaps the government will be enticed to call a new election. Certainly, they might be tempted to do anything that would stall implementation of the new policy on housing announced by the government, as reflected in these amendments.
The Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) has stated on many occasions that the amendments now being debated by the House represent the most progres-
March 22, 1973

sive social housing legislation to be undertaken to date by this government. I find it interesting to speculate on what might be happening. Are we so bold as to suspect that the thrust of these amendments may indicate a change in the preoccupation of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation with dwelling starts rather than with the actual social implications of the lack of a housing policy? We have all become aware that this financially and architecturally oriented institution appears to be more concerned about the number of houses being started, than about the actual housing problems facing the Canadian people, especially those who unfortunately are in the middle and low income brackets. It is refreshing again to speculate that perhaps this financially and architecturally oriented institution is about to be transformed into a sensitive social agency engaged in the development of new communities, the improvement of existing neighbourhoods, and the rehabilitation of existing substandard housing.
One area where I contend that this government and CMHC have completely fallen down is in the rehabilitation of existing neighbourhoods. We have all observed the effect of the bulldozer technique. We went through a period when the bulldozer seemed to be the answer to all of our housing problems-the answer to the large number of substandard housing units and substandard neighbourhoods that exist in this country. Now, of course, the government has realized that the bulldozer is not the answer, that perhaps rehabilitation does have a part to play in helping to solve the very serious and critical housing problems that exist today.
Again in my city of St. John's, there was a time back in the middle sixties when the government built up great expectations by designating areas for urban renewal schemes and urban renewal studies. Although great things were promised and great studies were undertaken, I am afraid very little action followed. This was because it was obvious then, as it is obvious now, that the bulldozer is not the answer; indeed it is far from the answer. Rehabilitation, a more sensitive attitude, a more humane approach to the problems of people living in older existing neighbourhoods, were what were required, rather than the so-called bulldozer technique and urban renewal studies undertaken during this period by the government and CMHC.
Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is, of course, the federal government's housing arm. But how can this agency presume to be effective when it continues to classify the Dennis report on low income housing as confidential, with distribution restricted to within CMHC? I have been told-and I hope that the minister will make a note of this-that the library at CMHC does not even have a reference copy of the Dennis report. How can that agency expect its staff to be aware of the social implications of the housing policy? This repressive attitude toward the control of information is unthinkable. This is ridiculous when you consider that the Dennis report is on sale in every bookstore in the country, but there is not even a copy of it in the CMHC library.
It is interesting to note the position with respect to the staff of CMHC. On October 3, 1972, the present minister promised that CMHC senior personnel would be replaced
National Housing Act
by those possessing skills more compatable to implementing social policy. It is ridiculous when you realize that the present president of CMHC, Mr. Hignett, continues to function in that role two years after his formal resignation. The president of CMHC, whose responsibility it is to give direction to Central Mortgage to implement the government's policy with respect to housing, continues to fill that role two years after he indicated to the government that he wished to retire from his position.
In the past year, there has been no change in the senior personnel of CMHC. Recent vacancies in the middle level have been filled from the present management complement. In other words, there has been absolutely no new blood injected into CMHC. Therefore, how can we expect that agency to operate under a president who has indicated his interest, desire, willingness and anxiety to retire and with no new personnel involved in the policy making or administration of CMHC, where vacancies are filled by people in the lower echelon of the corporation without new personnel or new blood being injected into the corporation? The minister will probably say that such changes are coming. He will probably tell the House that new appointments are to be made.
Perhaps a new president of CMHC will be appointed. Perhaps new personnel on the policy making level will be appointed, but these appointments should have been made before this legislation was introduced. These appointments should have been made prior to the implementation of these proposed amendments to the National Housing Act, especially when they are purported to constitute the government's presence in social housing legislation. I am not aware of any attempt having been made by the government or CMHC to change their attitude with respect to housing or talents. CMHC appears to have failed in its attempt to attract young people who are trained in the social science skills which a person working in that corporation requires.
The open hostility that exists between the Minister of State for Urban Affairs and CMHC's policy development unit has resulted in a sad waste of talent and expertise. This country cannot afford to suffer any longer from the minister's failure to define responsibilities. Either the minister should create a department of housing and urban affairs or he should let CMHC get on with its job. At any rate, this is a very serious problem that exists in Canada with respect to housing.
I would be remiss in my duty if I did not make reference to a situation that exists in my constituency. It is relative to CMHC and the government's formal policy of urban renewal. In the west end of my constituency, there is an area that is referred to as Mundy Pond. The government undertook a comprehensive program of urban renewal in this area. The program was announced with a great deal of flurry and fanfare. A great many promises were made to the people who live in that section of St. John's West. When the program was probably a little more than half completed, because of the escalation of costs, prices and contracts, the funds ran out. There was not sufficient money to complete the program as envisaged by the government and promised to the people of that area.
I understand that last year a group known as the Mundy Pond House Owners Association made representations to

March 22, 1973
National Housing Act
the minister with a view to acquiring additional funds to enable them to complete the Mundy Pond urban renewal scheme. I also understand that their request for additional funds was refused. This situation is a little ridiculous. The federal government saw fit to spend a large sum of money on this project and then refused to advance sufficient funds to enable the municipal and provincial governments to complete the job. The Mundy Pond area is probably typical of a large number of under-privileged substandard have-not areas in this country. It consists of people who are on the bottom half of the income ladder. Their income is far below the national average. Indeed, it is so low that without direct government assistance from the municipal and provincial governments, they cannot hope to attain the standard to which most Canadians have become accustomed and to which they are entitled.
These people have been forced to live and raise their families under conditions which in most parts of Canada would be looked upon as being far below the normal standard. Indeed, it would be unthinkable to expect these people to live and raise their families under the conditions which prevailed in that area prior to the commencement of the urban renewal scheme, yet this government refused to acknowledge its responsibility to complete the project as promised, to complete it in a manner that is consistent with that which is expected by all Canadians. This would be by providing decent and sanitary conditions under which they can live and raise their families. I would urge the minister to give some serious thought to the request of the people of Mundy Pond who are not asking for anything except the opportunity to complete the job in accordance with the promise of the government in respect of the urban renewal scheme that was started there some years ago.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING NEIGHBOURHOOD IMPROVEMENT, REHABILITATION, OWNERSHIP, NEW COMMUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I am aware of the fact that the mayor of St. John's and the provincial minister of urban affairs came to Ottawa to talk to the minister. I am aware also that more than a year ago a delegation came to Ottawa, before the minister assumed his present portfolio. This was a delegation from the Mundy Pond Householder's Association. They spoke to officials at CMHC and I believe the former minister. At that time their request was flatly refused. I hope the minister will find it possible to accede to their request and make sure that the scheme started by the government will be realized.
We find, Mr. Speaker, that there are very serious problems in housing in many parts of this country where neighbourhoods are being allowed to deteriorate almost

to the point of no return because there is insufficient interest and lack of funds provided by the government and CMHC to enable the neighbourhoods and older properties in our cities to be rehabilitated. While I do not wish to take away from some of the benefits in this new legislation, and while I do not want to downgrade the minister in respect of his efforts to bring about some kind of improvement in the housing legislation, I hope that his obvious interest will be reflected in the attitude of officials at CMHC, at the grassroots level, who will be required to administer the policies presented to the House by the minister.
I hope it will be possible for CMHC to develop a better liaison between its officials and the people whom they represent because I find in my city-and I suppose this may be typical of the situation in most cities-that the officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation appear to have adopted an attitude of being holier than thou, sitting in an ivory tower on their high pedestals. They do not get down to the level of the average people in our cities and provinces in respect of housing. I hope a better liaison can be developed between the officials of CMHC and the people in our cities who go to them for advice and help in respect of their housing problems.
With regard to the development of land, we all know that the cost of serviced building lots has reached a point where it is almost unrealistic for a person to endeavour to buy a lot on which to build a home. I contend that this problem has arisen because of the fact that there is an inadequate supply of serviced building lots in our cities. At the present time in the city of St. John's, the price of a building lot is anywhere from $10,000 to $15,000. I can think back to a time in the early and mid-1960's when, because of a land assembly program undertaken by the three levels of government, municipal, provincial and federal, building lots were selling at a reasonable price. Less than ten years ago one could buy a building lot in St. John's, Newfoundland for under $5,000. Today, because of the scarcity of serviced building lots, it is impossible to purchase a building lot for less than $10,000. Therefore I urge the minister to be very sympathetic and to be very generous in respect of our provincial and municipal authorities in their efforts to provide land assembly projects, which I contend would have the effect of lowering the over-all cost of building lots.
I would also strongly recommend to the minister and to the government that the minister endeavour to impress upon his colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), the need to abolish the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials. This is something which I consider to be overdue. A government which pretends to be interested in the housing problems of our country, a government which pretends to be interested in the lot of the salaried blue-collar Canadians in this country, surely should start putting its money where its mouth is, to use an old cliche. I believe one way to do it is to abolish the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials which would make new home ownership more accessible to the average low salaried person in our country today.
I am impressed by certain aspects of this legislation which I think are good. I believe the idea of encouraging co-operative housing is good. Certainly, the plan in
March 22, 1973

respect of developing and improving neighbourhoods is excellent. It should be pursued and taken advantage of by our cities and municipalities. I am encouraged by the new awareness shown by this government with regard to cooperative housing. This is one way in which people can roll up their shirt sleeves and hopefully solve their own housing problems. I commend the government for the initiative it has taken in this area.
In closing, I would again impress upon the minister and upon the House the need to complete the urban renewal schemes which were undertaken by the government. Particularly, in my case, I would commend to the minister the Mundy Pond renewal scheme. I hope he will be able to convince his colleagues in the cabinet that additional money is necessary to undertake the completion of that scheme as promised by CMHC. I hope they will allocate more funds and make more money available for the development of land, perhaps for the provision of land banks, call it what you want, but certainly I think we should do something to develop more building lots. I think this would have the effect of keeping prices down because the old law of supply and demand will prevail with respect to housing, just as it does to everything else. It is quite obvious that some definite action must be taken, some definite policy adopted, to bring about an end to the cruel and inhuman way in which a large number of our citizens are being treated.
There are certain parts of my riding where the conditions under which some people have to live are quite incredible in this day when we brag about the so-called just society and when we hear such slogans as "the land is strong". In some areas we see people living in substandard houses, and not far away from them we find people living in great luxury, people who can afford to drive expensive motor cars and who live in homes that are beyond the wildest dreams of most people. There is great unfairness and inequity in the fact that some people are forced to live in substandard conditions while others live in the lap of luxury. I contend that it is the responsibility of this government, and indeed of any government, to ensure that our people are given a chance to live and raise their families in decent houses.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in support of this bill, and in the few moments left to me this afternoon I want to make one or two observations about an aspect of the bill which I think will be of advantage to the preservation of the character of existing neighbourhoods in large urban centres. I see the provisions of this bill respecting loans to facilitate home ownership, the neighbourhood improvement program, and the residential rehabilitation assistance program as providing a bulk-ward against mindless redevelopment of the kind which has been going on all too frequently in a city like Toronto. Certainly, in my constituency of Lakeshore, which consists in large part of older homes, the provisions of this bill will, I hope, enable residents to maintain and preserve those homes and prevent this part of Toronto from being overrun by, as I say, the mindless redevelopment which is taking place in so many other parts of the city.
National Housing Act
Moreover, if that redevelopment can be forestalled and prevented and if the neighbourhoods can be preserved, those younger people who have grown up in that area, in that community, will, I hope, under the provisions of this bill find it somewhat easier to buy older homes in their neighbourhood. This would provide to that neighbourhood and that community another generation of community leadership which will, I fear, be lost if younger families must move farther and farther out of the older parts of the city into the suburbs in order to find housing at prices they can afford.
I hope, therefore, that when this bill gets to committee the minister will be in a position to provide us with more information than has been forthcoming so far. We will then be able to get some assurances that, for example, this bill will apply equally to existing as to new housing stock. Perhaps we can get some more concrete figures as to the income ranges to which the provisions of this bill will apply because I want to put in a word for those modest income families which comprise the great bulk of constituencies like my own and for whom, up to now, there has been not much in the way of assistance to enable them to own and preserve their own homes.
I would like from the minister, when we get into committee, some of the details which are apparently left to regulation at the present time. I would like to have some idea of what kind of assistance will be provided by the government by way of grants to enable families to maintain their monthly payments within tolerable limits. I hope that details of this kind will be tied to the act in such a way as to make sure that families in the modest income range will be able to benefit from its provisions. I do not want for a moment to deny the necessity of providing better housing for families in low income ranges, but I sometimes have the feeling that those in slightly better circumstances in the modest income ranges are overlooked in the drafting of legislation of this kind. I am disturbed at the suggestion-and I have heard it-that housing costs in a city like Toronto might be such as to render this program largely inoperative. Again, when the minister is before the committee I hope he can give us assurances that the kinds of income ranges and levels of assistance envisaged under this act will be such that residents of constituencies like Lakeshore, and there are many similar to it, will be able to benefit from the provisions of the act.
May I say in conclusion that there is in my riding a neighbourhood known as Laburnham which, over the last year and a half, has seen co-operation between the municipality and the residents of the area in designing a redevelopment program which preserves the character of the neighbourhood and which can greatly benefit, I hope, from the provisions of this bill. It is in the hope that not only that neighbourhood but others like it will in the future be preserved that I lend my support at this time to this bill.
