speakeroldname: Mr. J. M. Forrestall (Dartmouth-Halifax East) moved:
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF BRYDEN COMMITTEE REPORT
speechtext:
That an Order of the House do issue for the tabling of the Report of the Legislation Review Committee, chaired by John G. Bryden.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in the brief 20 minutes I have before me I should like to deal at the outset with perhaps one or two of the historical aspects that have led up to this position of stubbornness on the part of the government with respect to this most important report. A review of the historical aspects of something is important in the context of lapsed time between the acceptance of certain principles and their full implementation. No matter what we create it must be nurtured, fed and tended if it is to grow and expand, to keep pace with the growing demands of its day and environment.
I have ample evidence to suggest that in the immediate post-World War II period, employees of government began to feel strongly the changes of altered circumstances. The two paramount questions facing this House, the government, and indeed the country with respect to public employees were the twin questions of veterans preference, and the need to accommodate a greater linguistic balance within the public service. The Fair Employment Practices Act of some 20 years ago was another area that required change.
These matters preoccupied governments and the old Civil Service Association for a period of seven or eight years. As early as 1953, it was apparent to the then Prime Minister, the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, that further changes were absolutely necessary, changes which in his view had to be sweeping and all-embracing. They would

encompass major changes in concepts of government-employee relationships, and they were changes which he knew would be vigorously opposed by the Civil Service Commission of those days, indeed it might be said by the entrenched Civil Service Commission of those days. But he knew that changes had to come about if government and its growing civil service staff throughout the country were to function adequately. From this awareness on the part of the Prime Minister came the ground rules for what was to evolve during the next 12 to 14 years, during the days of the so-called 1954 secret committee and the Heeney Report, which will certainly be easily recalled by some distinguished members of this Chamber.
There was a reluctance in the early stages of committee meetings on the part of some members of the Civil Service Commission to look ahead. At that time there was a lukewarm chairman of the commission, and indeed Mr. Bryce expressed the fear that if changes did not come about quickly it might well be many years before sweeping conceptual changes could be brought about with respect to the public service. Regrettably, Mr. Speaker, his fears were well founded. It was some years before anything was accomplished. Indeed, some 14 years went by, and it was not until 1967 that change really came to the fore, although this is not to say that work was not being done during that time. A strong appeal has been made by opposition members during the last two years for the tabling or the release of the Bryden Committee Report. When undue delays occur in connection with something as complex as the rules and guidelines within which the public service operates, then there is great fear of entrenchment, of immobility on the part of governments, and of over-familiarity with known routines. A stance is adopted against making any movement. It is this which concerns us deeply.
As I say, it took 14 years before any basic changes were made. With the experience we have gained over the last five years, we have all the evidence that is necessary for any government, or any parliament, in order for it to institute an extension or a furtherance of the changes that were begun five years ago. There is recognizable merit in moving slowly in such complex areas as the relationships between a government and its employees. You have to be certain of the full consequences of change before making change. But caution should not result in procrastination in bringing about the many changes that are so necessary. What we are simply saying is that what has been done to this point in time has been good, but it is now time to do more with respect to the regulations under which governmental employees function.
The concept of full bargaining rights, although long shunned by the public service, particularly by certain levels within it, is now fully acceptable. Their fears have long since been abandoned. We have accepted that the changes made five years ago were good, and we know that further measures must now be taken. Numerous settlements arrived at over the last five years support that contention. The time in which settlements were arrived at has shortened.
About two years ago, probably in anticipation of the necessity to make further changes, the government asked Mr. John G. Bryden to review the two main legislative
March 22, 1973

acts in this area, not with a view necessarily to making recommendations to the government but in the context of their usefulness. Some of my colleagues will speak about the understandings that existed at that time with respect to what was going to happen to his report.
The point I would like to develop is that, apart from any recommendations it may contain, the report itself is of the greatest importance not only to the members of this House but to the members of the Public Service Alliance, to the Professional Institute of the Public Service, to the Union of National Defence Employees, and to all other public service groups in Canada. To keep the report hidden at this point in time is unreasonable. The government has had it in its possession for a year and a half, or two years. Surely, the government now knows what its position will be. Why does it not release the report so that other concerned people can decide, on the basis of the information it contains, what amendments should be made to the Public Service Staff Relations Act and to the Public Service Employment Act?
I have difficulty in understanding why the government will only go so far as to say that, when it is ready to introduce amendments, it will reconsider its position with respect to the tabling of the report. This makes no sense to anyone who wants the benefit of the informed views of Mr. Bryden. It is clear that at present there are not full collective bargaining rights. I am not necessarily trying to find a reason why the government will not table the report but rather I am trying, in a brief manner and not too casually, to reason why the report should be published.
It is clear, Mr. Speaker, that there is not full collective bargaining rights for the public service at the present time. Section 7 of the Public Service Staff Relations Act reads:
Nothing in this act shall be construed to affect the right or authority of the employer to determine the organization of the Public Service and to assign duties to and classify positions therein .. . thus eliminating any right of the employee or an agent of any group from negotiating with the employer standards, procedure and processes governing classification of an assignment of duties to positions, appraisals, promotions, demotions, transfers, lay-offs, reassignment and releases.
The whole spectrum is removed from the parameters of collective bargaining and collective bargaining cannot be fully enforced unless it is total. If a thing is arbitrable it should be negotiable and vice versa, but that is not the case.
With each new agreement we see the difficulty that various groups are having in choosing the arbitration route over the conciliation and strike route. Anyone who has followed collective bargaining in the public service is aware of the difficulties that seem to be growing. There is the increasing irritant of the absence of relief procedures, and failure to provide for adjudication procedures for classification, grievances. The confusion that arises leads to difficulty and some of this may arise from the fact that we have three quasi-judicial bodies involved in these matters-the PSSRA for adjudication, the Treasury Board for classification and the Public Service Commission for appeal purposes.
Public Service
It is no wonder that PIPS has called for the establishment of a ministry for the public service. We have a whole area of exclusions which should have been looked at long ago. Indeed, some considerable merit must attach to the thinking of the Alliance in its call for a classification review board within but separate from the Public Service Commission. This could well take the form suggested by the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) in Montreal a few weeks ago when he referred to areas of discrimination, for example, with respect to language-in any event, identifiable areas of discrimination. Possibly this is a reason we should have an independent national human rights commission in this country.
Government is no longer a unique employer in Canada, Mr. Speaker, and it can no longer set itself apart from the other large employers. The relationships between governments and their employees are so complex, so professional that a minister of the Crown must accept his responsibility to the people of Canada and the people who are employed in his departments, specifically or generally. I suspect that we may find something to this effect in the Bryden report when it comes before us. Government cannot continue as its own judge and jury; as the country's largest employer it must accept responsibility for leadership in the area of human rights and in many other areas. It must allow its employees access to grievance procedures, and, where discrimination is involved, to an independent human rights commission.
Lest I go too far into a rambling, somewhat philosophic dissertation, let me make some reference to the need to consider extension of some form of involvement in the decision-making processes respecting working conditions for the staffs of our own House of Commons, the Senate and the Governor General, for example. Many years ago when this matter was being debated my friend from Winnipeg wondered why this, the epitome of democracy, denied its employees one of the fundamental rights of a democratic society, the right to collectively form their views and express them to their employer. Perhaps someone in government should at least find out whether our employees would like to be organized. There are ways to do this which would assure the confidentiality of their views as individuals, whilst permitting their collective position to be known.
A lot of things are going to happen shortly which will highlight the necessity for government action. There is a very real belief that some 50,000 public employees in this country have the fundamental right to wage parity. Since 1934, we have been labouring under an archaic unprincipled philosophy of prevailing rates; that is to say, rates paid to government employees are on a par with similar job classifications in the surrounding area. It is difficult to believe that any government would maintain this unfair and unjust treatment of employees in the public service. The public service and Crown corporations ought to pay the same wages in Victoria as in St. John's, Newfoundland, in Halifax as in Winnipeg, Calgary or Toronto. Why is it that 50,000 public servants, 35,000 of whom are civilian employees with the Department of National Defence, can have a job in Yarmouth, Nova Scotia and be paid $1.85 less than the rate in Vancouver for the same type of work? How do we expect to achieve national unity and avoid divisiveness unless government accepts the respon-

March 22, 1973
Public Service
sibility for taking the lead? We cannot have national unity when a machinist in the dockyard in Halifax is getting $1.05 less than a machinist in Esquimalt. This condition will persist as long as this government operates in secrecy, behind the screen of confidential reports. If I had my way I would reduce to one dollar every fee paid for consultants reports by every department of government so long as those reports remain confidential and are not made available to Members of Parliament.
Let us get on with the necessary changes in the Public Service of Canada, and let us do this by looking at the Bryden report. What is in it that makes the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) afraid to release it? Neither the President of the Privy Council nor the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) is in the chamber, and perhaps this is an indication of their interest in what is going on and a measure of the true interest of the government in this matter. That is how they show their interest in the people who are true and loyal servants of the people of Canada.
Mr. ]ean-Robert Gauthier (Ottawa East): Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to rise this afternoon to speak on the question of staff relations in the public service as well as the Public Service Employment Act. This subject is of fundamental importance for a member of this House representing a riding such as mine located in the shadow of the Peace Tower.
Mr. Speaker, like my colleagues I think we are in a position of guessing with respect to the Bryden report because I do not know more about it than they do. I feel that the Bryden report has no special status among the many reports that are continuously prepared by officials and others for the benefit of the government in power to help them make enlightened decisions to administer this country with efficiency. Some will suggest that the government has neither the right nor the privilege to commission or have prepared any report liable to throw light on any important question and I am sure that by appointing a three-member committee presided, I was told, by the minister responsible, this government wanted to keep it self up-to-date on the possible amendments to the legislation governing federal civil servants.
In that regard, Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few comments on the way which I think bargaining could be carried on between employers and employees in the public service. It will be remembered that the government announced in the Speech from the Throne that it would introduce amendments to the Public Service Act and the Public Service Staff Relations Act.
Numerous favourable comments have been made in the press since last January 4. I think the public servants' optimism is justified in that field.
Obviously, the government does not intend to bring major amendments to the Public Service Act before having consultations with union leaders, with whom it will have discussions beforehand.
For many months-even many years I am told-since 1971, I think the Bryden report has been prepared; the

opposition has asked that it be tabled in the House. Many questions have been put on the order paper, including one by the hon. member for Darmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall), namely question No. 148 asking the government if it intends to publish the Bryden report, and if so when, if not why.
I believe that this request is only the last of many others that have been made in this connection in the House.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Reid) replied on that occasion that the drafting of the Bryden report was subject to the condition that the document was internal and confidential and for the exclusive use of the department through which the Public Service Staff Relations Board reports to Parliament. This is why it has not been made public. However, when the bill to amend the Public Service Staff Relations Act is introduced in the House, the government will decide, after looking at the situation, whether public interest makes it necessary to publish that report.
The President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) also replied to the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East, on January 12, 1973, "that the Bryden committee report had been submitted to the government for its advice", adding that "it was not intended upon the setting of the committee that the report would be made a public document".
Mr. Speaker, it should be desired to promote harmonious and productive relations between the employer and employee associations. On the other hand, I believe that the government is entitled to have studies and reports prepared in order to throw light on a situation and to provide for any contingency. Otherwise, people could charge the government with not availing itself of the tools that can be supplied by expert officials.
Nowadays, public men often pay more attention to the patterns of a policy than to the policy itself, and I believe that we should realize it is essential, before setting objectives-and that is the way I do define the word policy-to gather evidence and to avail ourselves of the expertise of the professional people in the public service.

In 1966, the government undertook to provide for the public servants of Canada a system of collective bargaining. Since public servants did not fall under the jurisdiction of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act administered by the Department of Labour and the Canada Labour Relations Board, nor under the several provincial statutes administered by the respective provincial departments of labour and provincial labour relations boards, it became necessary to introduce legislation to provide for such a system.
On April 25, 1966, the late Right Hon. L. B. Pearson, the then prime minister, moved the following resolution, as recorded on page 4242 of Hansard:
That is it expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the establishment of a system of collective bargaining applicable to employees in the public service of Canada and for the resolution of disputes that may arise in the negotiation or conclusion of collective agreements applicable to such employees; to establish a process for the presentation of grievances of employees arising in connection with their employment and to establish a system for the adjudication of grievances of employees; to provide for the
March 22, 1973

establishment of a board, to be known as the Public Service Staff Relations Board, which shall be responsible for the administration of the said measure and to provide further for the constitution and appointment of such other authorities, officers and employees as are required in connection with the administration of the said measure.
The then prime minister went on to say, as recorded at page 4244 of Hansard for April 25, 1966:
In developing this new legislation the government has had certain general objectives in mind: First, to protect the public interest; second, to respond in an understanding and responsible manner to the aims and aspirations of its organized employees; third, to preserve the capacity of the public service to function efficiently in serving the people of Canada and, fourth, to respect the principles underlying industrial relations law and practice in Canada.

It is an acknowledged fact that the passage, in 1967, of the Public Service Staff Relations Act and of the Public Service Employment Act was a real breakthrough in the field of hiring and staff relations practices in the public service. Better still, these acts have been recognized as models of their kind and many other countries have seen fit to copy them and sent representatives here to study them. These pieces of legislation have drawn the world's attention, and I understand that the delegates who have been observing their application in Canada found them in most cases forward-looking, original and progressive.

In many ways the Public Service Staff Relations Act has achieved the objectives that were expressed in 1966 by the then prime minister. Although the legislation has been in effect for less than six years, over 300 collective agreements have been concluded by direct negotiation. There were at least 300 collective bargaining agreements and only five were settled by the strike route. I think this is a good record. Nevertheless, the government does not take a nonchalant attitude toward strikes in the public service. On the contrary, the government is acutely aware of the impact of public service strikes and is most anxious to assure that every reasonable effort is made to conclude collective agreements with its employees without disruption of service.
Moreover, the government has undertaken a review of the Public Service Staff Relations Act. In announcing the review, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang), through whom the Public Service Staff Relations Board reports to parliament, said:
The system of collective bargaining under the Public Service Staff Relations Act has been functioning for almost four years and sufficient experience has been gained to warrant an analysis and assessment of the act at this time. All interested parties including employee organizations and government agencies and departments, will be invited to express their views and recommendations in writing. The intention is to provide a vehicle whereby the views of interested parties can be co-ordinated and assessed in order that the government may clearly identify areas of concern and determine if revision of the act is required.
This was at the beginning of the Bryden committee hearings.
Public Service

In my opinion, there should be a will to promote harmonious and productive relations between the employer and employee associations. This assumption does not negate in the least any possible conflicts. On the contrary, it should be admitted that disputes and conflicts will arise even under a sound system, but they reflect the positive climate that should prevail between the employer and employee representatives.
The settlement of conflicts between employers and employees depends largely on the spirit which will prevail during the resolution of those disputes. It is important that the legislation governing collective bargaining within the public service make it possible to settle disputes so that both parties involved may reach a satisfactory agreement which, through the solution of those problems, will reflect a responsible attitude.
However, let us not forget the major responsibility of the government and its employees which is to ensure an efficient service that meets the needs adequately. No staff relations system within the public service can be satisfactory if it does not take into account the legitimate and reasonable interests not only of the Canadian public but also those of the public servants.

On numerous occasions the government has expressed its intentions in regard to personnel relations. For example, on September 21, 1972, in an open letter to Mr. Barnes the executive director of the Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said:
In answer to your letter of September 6 setting out a number of questions of concern to the members of the Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada, let me assure you that the government is prepared to reconsider any legislation, on the basis of experience. As you know, the government and the Liberal Party have received numerous and varied expressions of opinion on the Public Service Staff Relations Act, the Public Service Employment Act and the Public Service Superannuation Act to which you have referred.
In regard to the Public Service Superannuation Act, you request my views relating to a full escalation formula which would maintain the relative value of pensioners' incomes when compared to those of persons continuing in the employ of the public service.

Mr. Speaker, the government is open to collective bargaining and intends to consider closely advantages which could result from amendments.
Because my time seems to be nearly up, Mr. Speaker, I should like to go back to one of my hon. colleague's remarks to the effect that there had been an effort to bring about linguistic balance in the public service. I am not aware whether the Bryden report deals with bilingualism; since my colleague mentioned it, I can do so as well. I believe he spoke of historical objectives and linguistic balance. Linguistic balance, Mr. Speaker, is something we must achieve. We are working to that end. It is an important measure, necessarily involving many difficulties, but it is an absolute objective for the public service, which is a bilingual institution.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few remarks on a matter that I consider to be of great importance to this country, that of institutional bilingualism. Bilingualism in

March 22, 1973
Public Service
the public service is recognized to be a deserving cause, and I would remind you that this is stated very clearly in section 2 of the Official Languages Act. To quote:
The English and French languages are the official languages of Canada for all purposes of the Parliament and Government of Canada...
The act also compels every federal department and agency to serve the public in both languages, not only in the national capital but in any area where there is a significant demand for this service.
In my opinion, it follows quite clearly from this that the government and the public service must make sure that the qualifications for some jobs include theoretical and practical knowledge of both official languages, French and English, so as to attain the objective of institutional bilingualism.
It is worth reminding the House, Mr. Speaker, that the Official Languages Act, which all parties supported in 1969, was intended as a tangible and concrete sequel to the original statement by the late right hon. Mr. Pearson in 1966, which was repeated by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).
The government and, in my opinion, the public service too, have remained conscious of these objectives and of the principles of justice and equity that must prevail, and have laid down guidelines along which the administration is to be brought to implement the principles I have just mentioned.
There can be no doubt that in such a complex and critical undertaking, these guidelines are open to different interpretations so that very often, unless we use all our goodwill to understand them correctly, they may give rise to misgivings that are not altogether justified.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to read a short paragraph from an article published in Le Droit on October 27, 1972, signed by Mr. Alain Duhamel and dealing with bilingualism, staff relations and the public service in general, and more particularly with negotiations concerning working conditions. Mr. Duhamel says, and I quote:
By dealing only or almost exclusively with bilingualism in the public service, area candidates dwelled on the most visible component of the climate of concern among public servants. It is unfortunate that the debate at the constituency level did not cover all the other aspects of the relationship between the government and its employees.
Bilingualism may have been one of the most discussed topics here in the last two years, and with good reason. There were calls for justice and for several other things. I am still wondering whether the complaints were founded. On reading Mr. Spicer's annual report, one would think that the other side should have complained instead of the one which claimed to have cause for alarm. I could read excerpts from Mr. Spicer's report on the matter, but it might be preferable to postpone that till later.
One thing interests me greatly: we must now tackle an important question, that of working conditions in the civil service, labour relations and employment criteria. It would seem that the government wishes to negotiate, review and perhaps change the law with a view to giving civil servants some recognition in the field of employ-

ment, vested rights, and the laws they are entitled to, in order to enable them to become first class employees- which they are-to be treated as such in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I observe there are one or two members who wish to speak so I shall make my remarks very brief. May I say it is not my intention to raise a point of order, but I do wish that we in this House were in order at this time. Because there is a Standing Order about a quorum, I hope that something might be done to make sure that we do have enough members here. It would be a shame to have this House adjourn, in view of the important business that is before us tonight, as I am not formally raising a point of order.
The motion before us is very simple and direct: it calls for the tabling of the Bryden report. I have on the order paper a similar motion which was debated a week ago, and therefore my support for this motion is very clear. I go along with the arguments made this afternoon by the mover of the motion before us today for this report to be tabled.
It seems to me that the public service and also parliament have the right to know what is in the Bryden report, which was made after an examination of the whole question of the Public Service Staff Relations Act. However, the debate this afternoon has only touched on that issue now and then: it has ranged over the whole question of the adequacy of our personnel relations and of the legislation governing the public service, so I want to say a word or two on that matter. Since I did not raise the other point of order to which I referred, I hope that no one will raise a point of order against my straying a little from the precise subject matter of the motion.
I feel that the time has come for the government to take a closer look at some of the grievances and complaints made by public servants. The whole question of how collective bargaining is working needs to be reviewed. In particular, the complaints that public servants have about certain matters relating to pensions should be given much more active consideration than they are receiving at the present time. Many improvements to the Public Service Superannuation Act itself need to be made. Then there is the burning question of the escalation of pensions after retirement which, in the case of public servants, is still limited to an annual increase of 2 per cent whereas in some other categories that limit has been removed. These are matters that ought to be dealt with without delay.
I want also to make a point regarding our employees in this very building. The hon. member for Ottawa East (Mr. Gauthier) correctly recounted some of the history behind the Public Service Staff Relations Act. He pointed out that under the direction of the late Mr. Pearson a bill was brought in and referred to a special committee. I remind him and the House that when that committee reported on the Public Service Staff Relations Act, it made a recommendation to the effect that something comparable should be established for employees of the House of Commons, the other place and the Library of Parliament.
As the hon. member for Ottawa East pointed out, prior to the passing of the Public Service Staff Relations Act
March 22, 1973

the only collective bargaining that we had in the federal field was that provided by what is now part V of the Canada Labour Code. But that did not cover public servants. Now we have the Public Service Staff Relations Act which does cover public servants-those who are, in effect, engaged by Treasury Board-but no such collective bargaining legislation covers employees of the House of Commons, the other place and the Library of Parliament. Their immediate employers seem to be the Commissioners of Internal Economy. Just as there is a Public Service Staff Relations Act to regulate labour relations between Treasury Board and public servants, in 1966, I believe it was, or perhaps in 1967, our committee felt there should be comparable arrangements for collective bargaining between the Commissioners of Internal Economy and the employees of the three entities that operate here on Parliament Hill.
I regret very much that that recommendation has been treated just as a pious sentiment and has lain dormant in the report all these years. I think the time has come to practise what we ourselves have proclaimed. Here we are, the Parliament of Canada: we say that the people in the private sector should have collective bargaining, that employees in the public sector and employees of the public service should also have collective bargaining, but for our own employees on this Hill no such arrangement exists. All we have is a pious recommendation. I think the time has come for something to be done about this situation.
At least I have enjoyed something this afternoon, Mr. Speaker. Most of us have the experience of getting up to speak and finding other hon. members walking out. Having drawn attention to the fact that a certain Standing Order should be observed, it has been my pleasure to see a few members come in while I was speaking, and I believe that we are now legally constituted.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to take a few moments to speak to this matter. I listened with great interest to my colleague and friend, the hon. member for Ottawa East (Mr. Gauthier), make what I thought was a magnificient defence of the status quo, a defence of the posture of inactivity. I think this, from a member who holds a seat in this area, is to be regretted. He said that the Bryden report may not have or did not have any special status but was typically an internal government report, a report to advise government. I want to say to my colleague through you, Mr. Speaker, that it may be that way to the government, because this sometimes characterizes their attitude toward the public service, but it certainly is not an ordinary report to the public servants themselves.
As I recollect the history of this report, having read it- though neither the hon. member nor I were here at the time-according to my understanding the public service staff associations were hurried into preparing their submissions for this particular committee because it was a matter of some urgency at the time for the government to deal with these matters. This urgency, which began some years ago, has now become mired in bureaucratic red tape of the kind that seems to characterize the govern-
Public Service
ment. One may suspect that these recommendations by an independent committee, following input from staff associations which speak for thousands and thousands of public servants, represented proposals so far reaching that the government did not have the stomach to face up to them. That is one of the possible reasons. Whatever the reason, the delay cannot be justified merely by saying this is an internal document, because this matter is important to the lives and future of many public servants not only in this area but in the whole of Canada.
At the meeting of the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates we had the pleasure of hearing the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) discuss the whole question of appeals when dealing with problems in connection with bilingualism. He said-I think I quote his words correctly-that generally speaking the Public Service Commission is a court of appeal from departmental decisions. He went on to say that the Public Service Commission has contact with people in connection with appeals involving the whole question of merit, but has nothing to do with appeals of cases which involve discipline.
We do not know this, but it may well be that the Bryden committee report recommended to the government that the jurisdiction of the Public Service Commission ought to be extended to matters of discipline within departments. It may have recommended that people who are dismissed or dealt with in any way from a disciplinary point of view ought to have the right of appeal to that court. For all we know, the committee report may have gone even further. It may have said that the Public Service Commission ought not to be the tribunal to which public servants look; that perhaps for all matters of appeal, whether they are with respect to discipline or merit, there ought to be an independent tribunal. We do not know that. None the less, these matters are important.
I suggest that not only should justice be done to public servants but it must appear to be done. I am sure that when public servants gather to discuss the relationship of themselves and their staff associations to their employer, they wonder whether justice is being done with respect to withholding something so fundamental, or whether it even appears to be done. I think they can be forgiven if they decide that justice is not being done. The procedure, as mentioned by the hon. member for Ottawa East (Mr. Gauthier), of continually evading or failing to answer questions on the production of the report makes them feel that they are not being looked after.
As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) said, the time has come when pensions ought to be dealt with and the whole matter of collective bargaining of public servants, and the parameters within which bargaining and negotiation take place, ought to be looked at. This report may well be an important document containing the views of a dedicated person after hearing the evidence which staff associations submitted in their briefs.
The hon. member for Ottawa East defended the status quo by quoting the Speech from the Throne, the catch-all of promises none of which has seen the light of day to any

March 22, 1973
Public Service
great extent in legislation. I tmnk it was on January 16 that I asked the President of the Treasury Board when he would bring forward the amendments to the public service acts. He said he would consult the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) and advise the House. He hoped it would be this session, but he was not sure. This indicates the rather low priority that the government places on the whole matter of improving the lot of public servants, not only in the national capital, but in all of Canada.
There is no doubt that when parliament passed the Public Service Staff Relations Act in March 1967, it was welcomed by the Public Service Alliance and by many individuals. It was a major step forward. It ought not to have been the last step forward, but to date it is almost the last step forward that has been taken.
I have always hoped that this matter would come forward and tnat Defore the public service staff associations were asked to examine the legislation promised in the Speech from the Throne they could examine the recommendations contained in the Bryden committee report. When the promised legislative changes are brought forward, public servants will be in a disadvantageous position. Their position certainly will not be advanced by the fact that the government has seen fit not to bring forward this matter. I think public servants and their associations would have been better served if this report had been made public.
The psychology of the government is not really of justice. With all due respect to the government, its stand on this matter is inexplicable in light of the circumstances and the importance of the government of Canada as the major employer in this country. No amount of soothing, syrupy, empty phrases or empty defences of the status quo by members opposite will justify the failure of the government to release this report.
Questions were asked on May 6, 1972, March 7, 1971, and in April, 1971, concerning the subject matter of the motion we are debating today. All these questions contained the simple request that the government produce the report. The government may or may not rely on the report, depending on its point of view, but in failing to produce it the government has done the public servants of Canada and their staff associations a disservice. I am sorry to have to say that.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING NEIGHBOURHOOD IMPROVEMENT, REHABILITATION, OWNERSHIP, NEW COMMUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the massive participation of my colleagues from all sides of the House to the debate on this bill proves that it bears on a capital problem which unfortunately has been neglected for too many years. To prove may point, may I be allowed to refer to an article published in the magazine Le Consom-mateur canadien (The Canadian Consumer) for April 1973, which proves that we are ahead of our times, as this is still the month of March. In this article entitled "Les consommateurs et le logement" (The Consumer and Housing), Mr. Speaker, the first paragraph reads as follows:
The average Canadian does not consider himself as a housing consumer. He certainly does for food, gasoline, clothing and daily services, but not at all for housing. This is something too substantial to be consumed. Furthermore, it is more a matter of investment for those who own a house. Most Canadians are used to capital gains from real estate to think about the cost of housing from a consumer's point of view.
Mr. Speaker, housing has been the exclusive field of builders or developers for too long. In many cases, builders have been incompetent and developers have been unscrupulous.
On Monday last, we heard the excellent speech made by the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Godin) who explained to us in revealing details how the poor consumer has to struggle against odds when he is buying land or against developers who are more interested in "making a buck" than in building houses properly. It is an inacceptable fact that he has to face the misunderstanding if not the dishonesty of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation management.
No wonder these housing sharks undertake lawsuits which are as ridiculous as they are enormous. We are aware that my colleague from Portneuf is being sued for $500,000 with both the CBC and the newspaper Le Soleil, by a Quebec area homebuilder.
As it is obvious that the small wage earners are having difficulties in the housing field, and there is also the fact that my colleague from Portneuf is now feeling the consequences.
Why is it so? Let me refer once more to the article I was speaking aDout a few moments ago. The second paragraph states, and I quote:
Housing is undoubtedly a consumer item. It is something everybody needs and has to use, under one form or another. It is something which costs money in one way or another. It is also an item which absorbs usually between 25 and 30 per cent of the family income in Canadian cities. As a matter of fact, housing represents one third in the consumer price index. At times, in low income families-
[Mr. Baker.J
March 22, 1973

This is, Mr. Speaker, I believe, the important point of the paragraph I am reading.
I continue to quote:
-who do not live in public housing, it may swallow up to half of the family resources. The general rule according to which "the poor is the one who pays more", applies very well to housing, because compared to middle income families, those who are in the 20 per cent bracket at the bottom of the income scale spend twice as much for housing.
The average housewife or head of the family is not as well informed or in as good a position about housing costs as about the prices of cars, groceries, drinks or dry cleaning. Even though a house might be the most important purchase they do during their life, it is the item of their budget on which they have the least degree of control. The same is true when it comes to renting a place to live.
The fact that buying a house or renting a place to live are not everyday occurrencies puts the consumer, either single or married, in a position twice as vulnerable. If we were to buy a house every month or even every year, we would behave more like housing consumers. We would begin to know in what way the dice are loaded against the purchaser: the consumer.
Thus, Mr. Speaker, low income groups are being pushed around. They take for granted that there is nothing they can do about it and let each and everyone meddle in the field of housing, almost without complaining. How could it be otherwise when one sees that even government organizations fail to protect their interests. And in order to support that allegation, Mr. Speaker, I will refer once again to that article, the value of which cannot be put in question since it was written by the senior consultant of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in Ottawa.
Thus, I wonder how it is that the senior consultant of the CMHC sees problems just like we do ourselves and that effective programs in that area are still on the drawing board.
In this respect, Mr. Speaker, may I quote an important paragraph from the article written by the senior advisor of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation:
For instance, let us simply look at two aspects of the National Housing Act in relation to the consumer. If you buy a new house with a mortgage loan under the Act, an inspector will come and look at the project at least three times during construction. The point is that he does not come to protect you, but to protect the creditor who provides the loan. As a buyer, you have no formal guarantee as to materials and labour, but you may of course hire an inspector or an expert at your own expense. When you buy an automobile, a refrigerator or a television set, you get a guarantee that protects you to a degree, but you get no guarantee when you buy a house that is much more expensive and is paid over a much longer period.
It is almost unbelievable, Mr. Speaker, to find that one of the senior advisers of a corporation which is directly connected to the Department of Urban Affairs gives valuable advice to the minister when saying: Your legislation is not meant for people with a low income; it does not assist the man who earns an average salary or income. The law does not protect them at all. On the contrary, it merely protects the investors, the creditors, the people who have capital and make it profit.
Mr. Speaker, this situation is ridiculous and, again, when we find that some people in the right place are capable of giving appropriate advice, we are truly wondering.

National Housing Act
At the risk of being lengthy, I should like to quote another paragraph of Mr. Laidlaw's comments which support my view:
If you obtain a mortgage loan under the same act, you must make a down payment of 1 per cent... of the total amount of the loan, to be paid into the Mortgage Insurance Fund controlled by the CMHC. For whose protection? The buyer's? Not at all. The purpose of the fund is to protect the lender if necessary. But, and there is the rub, you make this payment even though the lender is already holding a mortgage on the property. It seems strange that consumers seem never to have wondered about this. It could be thought that if lenders need additional protection over and above the mortgage it would be up to them to finance it. It could also happen that consumers might wonder why they are called upon to pay for protection to lenders. In an editorial in the October 28 issue of the Financial Post, it is pointed out that the MIF has now gone over the impressive figure of $300 million, "whereas" applications for compensation have reached only $10 million. Consumers have shown themselves to be willing contributors to the consolidation of mortgage loan operations.
Mr. Speaker, I cannot overstress, and I hope the minister is paying carefull attention, my astonishment over the fact that a public servant, a senior adviser of the CMHC should make such recommendations without our having had the proper reaction before today.
I sincerely hope the bill we are to consider will correct this. I also hope, Mr. Speaker, that in this field as in all others, policies truly geared to the people will finally be implemented. It is evident that housing is a very vulnerable point for Canadians and that housing is not something you can do without.
Whether we like it or not, Mr. Speaker, we have to have shelter, especially in a country like ours where life is a constant struggle against the elements. That is no doubt what brings, once again, the CMHC's chief adviser to write the following, and I quote:
Housing is a field in which demand is constant, and the average consumer is especially vulnerable. To begin with, it is not something optional, least of all in the Canadian climate. Also, not only is it a highly complex field involving economic, social, legal and regulation factors at various levels, but also the consumer's choice is very limited. An average family can easily find itself caught in a situation from which it is very hard to escape: legal texts tend to be irrevocable, moving is expensive and takes its toll on family life, and social barriers often can not be broken down. Nobody can choose where he is going to live as freely as he can choose a car.
Mr. Speaker, I think we can see from these few paragraphs of the article just how deeply Canada has been affected by the housing question. I might congratulate the minister on having become aware of this very acute problem, in the light of which Bill C-133 now before us deserves our closest attention.
There are in fact economic and social factors to complicate the finest principles a bill can contain. One can therefore come to ask oneself to what extent Bill C-133 can fill in the gaps we have seen.
I should like at this point, Mr. Speaker, to take the case of the province of Quebec, which for years-and nothing was done about it until five or six years ago-has been apart from the other provinces as far as housing and homes are concerned. I remember quite well that even 15 or 20 years ago Central Mortgage and Housing was refusing almost every loan application from potential home owners in the province of Quebec, and it was not because

March 22, 1973
National Housing Act
oi racial or linguistic discrimination but merely because housing concepts are different in a country where regions are quite different one from the other.
For one loan granted in the province of Quebec, 50 or 100 were granted in Ontario. Why? Simply because those setting out the housing standards and regulations were acting on the basis of an Anglo-Saxon concept. It is as simple as that, Mr. Speaker, and at that time the administration of the act became impossible. How can you justify that?
Today the problem is perhaps less extensive but I think here again that the legislation should take into account the difference between regions in the field of housing. It must be recognized that the French Canadian in Saint-Marc-des-Carrieres or Portneuf does not perhaps have exactly the same concept of housing than the man in Edmonton or Vancouver. Then it would not be necessary to legislate and impose regulations which go against his own individual thinking.
The result has been a certain kind of discrimination which was not deliberate, however in the future this will have to be totally remedied.
There is another problem that must also be considered when discussing a question such as this and still in connection with the province of Quebec, Mr. Speaker; people are very poorly informed about the benefits of federal legislation.
I wonder, for example, to what extent municipalities in Quebec are aware of the fact that Central Mortgage and Housing can help them solve their sewage disposal problems and all sorts of other problems relating to housing.
Then, I reflect that the minister should have public relations officers whose responsibility would be to explain to the municipalities, in the province of Quebec in particular, all the possibilities contained in the act, and I am anxious that this new act is passed so that it can be used.
This is what occurred in Quebec, I think. The advantages offered in some federal acts, because of continuing constitutional disputes, end up being ignored by Quebecers. There again, the victims are the common people. Therefore, I wonder whether, in such a situation, the minister should not consider having very specific information distributed and see to it that his departmental officials are prepared to inform the municipalities.
Here is another point with which I should like to deal also. The importance of urban centres like Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver, among others, is generally acknowledged, but more and more villages and small towns are being forgotten, which is most unfortunate. Many of our current problems, especially housing problems, simply result from excessive centralization, and should the government policy make for even greater centralization, where will that lead us?
We want to control pollution, to preserve our environment, and we keep doing every thing to promote further deterioration of some demographically strategic centres. In fact, any housing policy likely to encourage decentralization should be supported, because such a goal is extremely important. Increased decentralization will result, by the same token, in investors being urged to

diversify their investments, which will serve the best interests of the people.
Mr. Speaker, the article I was just quoting is quite important and I would advise the minister to have frequent meetings with his main adviser from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, who will explain to him how to come up with an adequate piece of legislation.
Some will say that as a matter of fact Bill C-133 will remedy all the shortcomings in the housing field. However, we all know that perhaps the most important thing will be the regulations that will follow as everything depends upon them. If they are not drawn up as they should, the legislation might be inadequate and even the best provisions of this bill will be useless.
This is what motivates my being in agreement with the Social Development Council of Canada. In its memorandum to all hon. members, on January 30, 1973, this Council seems to have grasped the problem quite accurately. In fact, its criticisms of Bill C-133, are accompanied with recommendations and general comments with which I am in general agreement.
Let me quote a few excerpts from the brief we received from this organization:
The housing committee of the CCSD finds that Bill C-133 includes a number of remarkable amendments that will make it a better legislation than the former one.
That is at least something!
And I quote further:
-We are particularly happy that the compulsory sharing of costs by provinces and municipalities has been removed from most programs, that important and new provisions on co-operative housing and on new communities have been added, that the leasing of land development areas is facilitated and that the development of lands outside neighbourhood improvement areas is provided for.
We are still wondering how this bill will truly improve housing condition for low income groups. This is a persistent concern because these amounts of the grants-which are determining factor in order to know whether the proposed programs will be beneficial to the low income groups-are not specified generally in the bill and are left for regulations. In the committee's opinion, Parliament rather than this government should determine who will benefit from state-subsidized programs. We, therefore, believe that as far as possible the amounts of the proposed assistance should be stated in the bill.
It will be easily understood therefore, that I make the same reservations as the Canadian Council on Social Development with regard to this bill.
We recognize that the principles stated in Bill C-133 seem to be excellent but we are wondering about its lack of precision. How will it be remedied? As a matter of fact, senior officials of the department will be the ones to enact those regulations. And that is why we are in expectancy and are wondering what will be those regulations exactly.
In concluding my remarks, I also agree with the following remarks in the submission which was presented to us:
Since the new housing programs are only outlined in this bill and it is obvious that their success or failure will mostly depend on the relevancy of the regulations under the act, we urge the Minister of State for Urban Affairs to conduct extensive consultations on the drafting of the regulations, not only with provincial and municipal housing authorities and the building industry, but also

Unfortunately, in this country it is not uncommon to see 25 per cent to 30 per cent, or even more of the family income eaten up by this cost. It is a fact that one-third of the consumer price index is represented by the cost of housing.
It is a sorry state, Mr. Speaker, when statistics verify that compared to the average, people in the lowest 20 per cent of income category in this country spend twice the proportion of their income for shelter as those at the other end of the scale. The exceptions, of course, are the low income families who have been able to secure far too little of the public housing that is available.
No consumer is more vulnerable than the home purchaser. If he had to buy a house every month, or even once a year, he would be much more aware of how great the odds are against him in buying a home. Events in the past few years have indicated a growing awareness and
National Housing Act
concern about the cost of cars, groceries and various food stuffs. And, Mr. Speaker, when I indicate that the scales are tipped against the buyer, consider for example just two aspects of the present National Housing Act in relation to the consumer. If you are buying a new home with a National Housing Act mortgage loan, an inspector will call at least three times during construction to examine the work in progress. To protect you is not his prime aim; his aim is to protect the lender who is providing the loan. As a purchaser, you get no firm guarantee of the materials and workmanship. You may hire an inspector or examiner on your own, but this is very seldom done. At least when you buy a car or a television set there is some kind of guarantee that gives you a measure of protection, but there is no firm guarantee when you take on the much costlier, long time purchase of a home. In most cases it is the most important purchase made in a person's lifetime.
Now, Mr. Speaker, add to this the fact that presently a 1 per cent premium is charged on the total loan as mortgage insurance held in trust and managed by Central Mortgage and Housing. One has to ask, for whose protection are you paying this 1 per cent? Are you paying for yourself as a buyer? No; the mortgage insurance fund is for the protection of the lender in case of default. But you, the buyer, pay the premium even though the lender already holds your mortgage. Consumers, strangely enough, never seem to question this arrangement. One would imagine that money lenders, if they needed extra protection over and above the mortgages that they hold, would provide it themselves at their own expense, or that consumers would at least question why they must pay so directly for safeguards for the lenders. On October 28 an editorial in the Financial Post pointed out that the mortgage insurance fund is now worth an impressive $300 million, while claims against it are only $10 million. Consumers have certainly paid well to ensure the operation of mortgage lenders.
So badly dealt with has been the consumer of housing or shelter that it is accurate to describe the consumer as a chap with hat in his hand, asking for this consideration or that consideration even though he is the one who is paying at every turn. This kind of ridiculous situation has made the consumer slowly more aware of the collective power that is needed for his own protection. We have seen this already in tenants' associations, where a united front has been presented to bargain with landlords. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the few minutes allotted to me, I wish to draw the attention of hon. members on the serious problems which will remain in the housing field as a result of the inadequacies of the bill now under consideration.
The government recognizes the importance not to say the urgency of a speedy intervention to solve that major problem for all citizens, but once again it is unable to carry out the essential steps. Instead of grappling with the basic issue, it merely beats about the bush and amends the existing legislation.
The Canadians were not expecting the misgivings and half-measures in which the government delights. The Canadians are demanding an opportunity to live in decent dwellings at decent prices, which is in no way guaranteed in Bill C-133.
In some countries enjoying a tropical climate with sunshine and hot weather, a house is not a necessity.
In Canada, during the winter months, it is necessary to have not only a roof, but also walls and windows which keep the heat inside and keep the proverbial cold of the Canadian winter from sneaking in.
Of course, some well-to-do people follow migrating birds and, away from the cold, lounge around on the

March 22, 1973
National Housing Act
beaches of Florida or somewhere else, but the vast majority of Canadians must put up with the severity of our climate. It is therefore absolutely necessary that all these people may enjoy the protection of a decent house built to withstand wintry cold.
Unfortunately, the current situation falls far short of this need. In the report from the Senate special committee on poverty, one can read as follows:
Task Force on Housing and Urban Development estimated there were 5,500,000 housing units in existence in Canada in 1968. Half a million of these were substandard.
I insist -on this, half a million housing units were substandard. This means therefore that out of the 5,500,000 housing units in existence in Canada, half a million were below standards established on the basis of climate or social environment.
But that is not all. Coming back to the poverty report, and I quote:
The number of families and individuals requiring housing is 5,700,000. It is as simple as that.
The Task Force also noted that a minimum of 200,000 housing starts would be required between 1969 and 1973 simply to maintain the existing situation.
And yet, in 1970 alone, 190,528 housing starts have been made. So this means that over 200,000 Canadians are now deprived of housing while over half a million live in dwellings quite inadequate in view of our harsh climate.
This is a real scandal and despite its half measures and patchwork measures the government will fail to hush it up. When we know that over 700,000 Canadians or Canadian families are without a home, the time is long past for amending or patching up legislation which has helped such a situation to continue.
The government must deal with the disastrous housing situation with measures in keeping with the urgency and the seriousness of the problem.
Here are some measures that the government could have taken had it really wanted to get down to the roots of the unrest in the housing sector.
The government must first understand that for the average citizen the building of a house involves the purchase of land. If he must lay out $5,000 or $10,000 to buy the land, how will he then be able to cover the cost of the building and the materials if he does not earn a prime minister's salary? How will he be able to build his house if the cost of the land exceeds the amount he has available?
He never will unless the government undertakes to set up land banks for resale at reasonable prices and on conditions acceptable to citizens who wish to build their home. This first measure would result in bringing home building within closer reach of everyone and contribute to stop this despicable speculation which is flourishing in real estate.
The barons of the industry who "play" with land values and create artificial shortages to gratify their cupidity make exaggerated profits from the population. Real estate profits have gone up by over 54.8 per cent from 1971 to 1972. Such an increase in profits is improper and reflects excesses in this field.

So the government must protect the citizens against speculators, and the setting up of land banks for citizens who wish to build a home despite their limited salary is a solution which immediately comes to mind.
But the citizen who is lucky enough to get a lot for a good price has not overcome all the difficulties yet, far from it. He must buy the materials which will be used to build the house. So, he finds out that he must pay an 11 per cent sales tax on those building materials, a higher tax than the levy on luxury articles. One would imagine that for the government housing is a luxury.
It is true that when one is stretched out on a beach in Florida one does not realize that in winter a house is quite important.
The Creditistes have fought against that 11 per cent tax on building materials for a long time because they know it keeps thousands of Canadians from affording decent housing. The government alone is responsible for that situation. It knows that this tax has an extremely negative effect on all those who would like to build a house but who cannot afford to pay more than one tenth of its value.
The increase in the cost of building materials is also added to the 11 per cent tax. By the way, it might be pointed out that manufacturers and retailers of these materials have seen their profits go up by 35.8 per cent between 1971 and 1972. This considerable increase in their profits also came from the pocket of the average citizen and that is another scandal.
As can he seen, the government and their good friends the building speculators are doing quite well. The government is getting richer through the 11 per cent tax while the large builders increase their annual profits in proportions out of reach of the imagination.
I once again urge the government to eliminate the 11 per cent tax on building materials. Building a house is no luxury and the government must understand it.
In that area again, the problems of the citizen who wishes to build a home are not over. If he is a low or middle income worker, he will have to borrow the money which will allow him to provide his family with a home. He is then confronted by the most absurd stupidity of our present system. Since interest rates are spiralling at a speed which evades governmental control, the citizen will have to pay more than four times the value of his house over the years.
With the present interest rate, a $18,000 house costs between $52,000 and $53,000 to the owner over 25 years, and $75,000 over 40 years. A $20,000 house will cost $58,000 over 25 years and approximately $84,000 over 40 years.
This situation is tearful. Of course, the usurers who shamelessly take advantage of the scarcity of money find it laughable because they benefit from the system.
A man runs into debt for 40 years simply to provide his family with a home for which he will pay three or four times its real value, and some people think this is normal.
But we have not yet reached the utmost degree of stupidity in this area. When a person has to run into debt for 40 years in order to pay for a house that is guaranteed
March 22, 1973

only for a period of 20 years under present standards, we reach the most incredible aspect of the present system.
We grant a 40-year loan to someone so that he can buy a house designed to last 20 years, and some people think this is normal.
The leader of the Social Credit Party (Mr. Caouette) is perfectly right in stating that under the present system, you mortgage tomorrow's salary so that you can buy today products that were made yesterday.
Mr. Speaker, it is inconceivable that a system which tolerates such absurdities can go on poisoning the lives of millions of citizens who normally should have access to the resources of our country. The government should lend an ear to the thousands of Canadian families which are deprived of the bare necessity, namely, a home.
Here are three measures which the Social Credit Party of Canada has proposed to all Canadians throughout the electoral campaign, and I want to remind the government of them today, so that it may consider the true wishes and needs of the Canadian people. I quote:
First:
(1)	Promotion of single family dwelling construction through guaranteed long term loans at a maximum interest rate of 3 per cent...
(2)	The owners of single family dwelling will also be eligible for an income tax deduction not exceeding the amount of their mortgage interest and the total of their municipal and school taxes, that reduction being limited however to $1,000 a year ...

The Canadian people are tired of waiting for legislation that meet their needs. They are fed up with half measures and hesitations. They are fed up with band-aid and patchwork. What they want-and the Creditiste say it again and again to the government-are measures which will enable all Canadians to live in decent and adequate housing suited to our severe climate, and also measures which will not require individuals to go into debt for 40 years and pay four or five times the price of the house he wants to build or buy.
This is what we ask of the government, Mr. Speaker, and we make this request on behalf of half a million homeless people forgotten by the government.

Mr. Speaker, although there are some good features in this bill it falls short of meeting the real needs of housing and urban development in Canada at the present time. I must, of course, applaud the good features. Most of them-in fact, I think all of them- were recommended in the report of the task force on housing and urban development four years ago. Consequently, I am delighted and would be churlish if I did not congratulate the minister for finally seeing the light and introducing some very necessary amendments that should have been made many years ago.
In order to meet the real needs of the Canadian people, however, we will require a much more comprehensive and effective approach. The housing situation in Canada has deteriorated very considerably since the mid-1950s. In the mid-1950s a working man with a decent wage could aspire to the ownership of a house. Today, in most parts of Canada, that is out of the question. As the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) pointed out last Thursday in his speech on behalf of this party, according to a study released recently by the Urban Development Institute of Canada, in 1961 an annual wage of $5,284 was needed to buy a house. This reflective figure was prepared by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. In 1971 an income of $16,623 was needed to buy a house, and only 4 per cent of the population could afford it. This is really a shocking situation, one that is totally unacceptable for Canada. It is a prospect that must really depress the average working person in this country. So rather than making progress since the mid-1950s, we have slipped, and slipped badly, and something must be done about it.
The cheapest new house available in some of our bigger cities today is in the range of $38,000 to $40,000. A front page newspaper article in one of the Ottawa papers tonight indicates that the average single family dwelling in Ottawa costs $39,000. In Toronto, the cheapest row house, or town house as they are called, costs about $38,000. The other area of cost, of course, is in the field of construction. These costs are not as great as the costs in respect of land and money, in so far as their flexibility is concerned, but they are still significant. One of the elements is the cost of labour. I think it is worth pointing out again that the rates of wages for construction workers have been rising faster than the average productivity of Canada. I have an example which I think will illustrate this point. In Hamilton, union labourers and union carpenters had the following rates over the last few years. First of all let us take labourers. In 1965 the rate was $2.44 an hour; in 1966 it was $2.65; in 1967 it was $2.86; in 1968 it was $3.20; in 1969 it was $3.95; in 1970 it was $4.52; in 1971 it was $575. and in 1972 it was $6.80. This is an increase of 180 per cent in that period.
Then we have the rates in respect of carpenters. In 1965 the rate was $3.60; in 1966 it was $3.90; in 1967 it was $4.22; in 1968 it was $4.66; in 1969 it was $5.00; in 1970 it was $5.40; in 1971 it was $7.82 and in 1972 it was $8.51. This
National Housing Act
represents an increase of 135 per cent over the period. This rate of increase is well in excess of the average increase in productivity in Canada and does raise a problem in that it contributes to the escalating cost and the maintenance of housing.
Then there is a personal example which illustrates the dilemma. Two hours work by a plumber, and just a tiny bit of material, entailed a bill of $50. For many Canadians that would represent the major part of the take-home pay for a whole week. It underlines, I believe, the dilemma of a very large proportion of the Canadian public who not only will be unable to acquire satisfactory housing but, if they should be able to acquire it, will be unable to maintain it in a satisfactory way.
The cost of housing obviously is out of line for people with low incomes. This raises the whole problem of maldistribution of income in Canada. I have a table from the returns of the Department of National Revenue which suggests that there are 4,975,000 Canadians with an income of less than $5,000 a year. In other words, over half of the work force of Canada has an income of less than $5,000. For all these people, the problem of providing adequate housing is very grave. In no case would one of these people be able to acquire a new house at existing prices. If some of them already own a house, they will have the difficulty of maintaining it to an adequate standard because of the high cost to which I have already referred. We must increase these low incomes. In my opinion, this is impossible without wage and price controls. In my opinion, it is inevitable that we will have to face this problem. We cannot sweep it under the rug indefinitely.
I have mentioned some of the experience in so far as incomes are concerned. Let me now indicate what will happen if we project some wage rates from now to the year 2000. Recently, in a speech to the Housing and Urban Development Association of Canada I said that the present minimum wage in Prince Edward Island is $1.10 an hour. The present wage of many construction workers is $8.00. If you compound those two rates to the end of the century at 8 per cent annually, by the year 2000 the minimum wage in Prince Edward Island will be $8.80 and the construction worker will be earning $63.91 an hour.
It would be totally impossible for people earning $8, $10 or $12 an hour in the year 2000 to buy or maintain houses built and serviced by people earning $63 or $65 an hour. To refuse to come to grips with this fundamental economic problem is, to my mind, totally irresponsible on the part of the government.
