I shall take the opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to make some comments on this bill which to my mind is definitely one of the most important for the future of each Canadian, particularly those who want to own a house.
I should like to say at the outset of my remarks that the bill in itself is not necessarily bad; on the contrary, I think it deals with certain very particular and important points. Now I have serious doubts as to whether this bill will fall short of its objective. Several comments have been made on the shortcomings in this bill and certain rather interesting suggestions and proposals have also been made, I think.
We try to make it easier to get a loan and particular attention is given to co-operative organizations.
Such changes have been required for a long time.
We are however aware of the difficulties met by the individual wishing to become an owner, given the economic conditions which are extremely hard in this country.
I shall limit myself to a few comments so that others may have time to express their views but just the same I would like to recall certain matters to the mind of the minister responsible since he is in the House and paying great attention to all the comments and suggestions.
I would like to go one step beyond criticism and invite the minister to consider one specific aspect. I said two years ago, I think, that it was important that the minister responsible for housing meet as soon as possible with all those directly or indirectly connected with the construction industry. At that time things were not going too well in construction. Those difficulties were due in part to strikes. The climate seems to have smoothed off now. The fact still remains that construction costs have increased considerably.
The recommendation I made two years ago is more pressing than ever. I would like to take this opportunity to suggest to the hon. minister that he should meet with labour unions, construction material manufacturers and, finally, with representatives of the whole sector related to construction.
If we are to really give a chance to the man who wants to buy a house it is absolutely essential not to facilitate access to loans with the interest rates we now have. I think this is just prolonging the agony of the individual as was done in the last five years in other fields. It is important to reduce the cost of houses to allow the individual to become a home-owner. The social impact of it is this: the owner becomes more socially active due to the fact that he is more interested in his own municipality and in his country.
Absolutely no mention is made of the repeal of the sales tax of 11 per cent on building materials and yet heaven knows if different parties have asked for it. I for one
National Housing Act
believe that that would have been a truly positive measure to reduce the cost of houses and made it easier for the individual to acquire ownership.
As I said before it is not with easier loans at present interest rates that we are going to reach that goal and allow those people who wish and are capable of doing so to become home owners. I think the emphasis should be put on reducing the cost of houses. The abolition of the sales tax on building materials would be truly advantageous.
Then the minister would have to have obtain sufficient funds to meet any possible demands. We know perfectly well that a great many applications would reach him.
A meeting should be held with the union representatives and the manufacturers of building materials. Since the minister has shown such interest for the objectives that all members pursue in this House concerning housing, he could in return impose certain requirements. They could discuss with the unions a suspension of the right to strike for perhaps five years. Imagine a five year period during which credits would be almost unlimited; imagine also the abolition of the sales tax on building materials. This would call for the suspension of the right to strike and a freeze on wages and on the price of building materials so that at last the future homeowner might benefit directly from this aid which could be granted by Parliament.
We perfectly know that if no condition were set, the contractor or the building material industry could often take advantage of this reduction which normally should benefit the owner.
We had better consider seriously such a proposal so that the citizen who wants to build a home can benefit from the reduction. The government has been accused of simply having extended the loan repayment period and it is always the same thing. As the hon. member for Shef-ford (Mr. Rondeau) indicated yesterday, on a loan of $30,000 at an interest rate of 9 per cent, for a period of 25 years, the repayment comes to $74,524. As far as I am concerned, with the legislation as it is now there is no way out.
I should also like that particular consideration be given to those who want to build a house and who, because of the location of their lot cannot benefit from public utilities. In a constituency like mine for instance some heads of families would gladly give a lot to their children but for lack of municipal services, these young couples are not eligible to CMHC loans. I think there would be an advantage in letting these people get loans from CMHC even though the land there is not serviced.
At the moment, the regulation governing that category of people is an encouragement to the municipality to crowd population into the large centres, leading to a centralization that we have paid a high enough price for so far in certain other fields. And a young couple who could get a lot free from their parents would be at an advantage from the start.
I therefore think the minister could increase the effectiveness of his bill by taking this factor into account. He would only have to meet with the builders, set out the

March 22, 1973
National Housing Act
standards, and supply the necessary funds. Some will object: Where are these funds to come from? Yet money is always found to free Canada of a serious problem, so I should think that this bill, which aims to remedy a nationwide problem, ought to be planned in such a way as to be effective.
The present bill is not bad in itself, and I shall support it, although it is totally inadequate to achieve the purpose that it seems to have set itself. It is all right for some members to say that it is a big step forward towards helping the future house-owner, but I think nevertheless that we could have done a lot more to rectify so alarming a situation.
I do not say the government has not tried to rectify the situation. The government has made capital investments which nevertheless ended in failure. You need only remember the problems of unemployment and inflation which were dealt with in all their aspects, with totally inadequate results. Much money was spent, but because it was used improperly, the result was failures.
Now the House has before it a bill on housing, but in order to make it more effective hon. members should join together and force the minister to understand my few suggestions, as well as those made by other hon. members about the 11 percent tax on building materials, and the repeal of this tax would be a great improvement over the present situation.
Of course, the government will lose some revenue; that is always the question we are asked. The government will lose revenue but on the other hand, if housing is doing well, building materials will sell more. That will stimulate the building materials industry. People will work, pay income tax, which is not the case today with the unduly high number of unemployed.
I think that one should not be satisfied with asking where money will be found if the 11 percent sales tax on building materials is removed. It is nevertheless possible to implement a policy which might be profitable to the government and do justice to those who are entitled to become homeowners.
Once again, I will restrict myself to those remarks. I hope they will be taken into consideration by the responsible minister. I hope they will be endorsed by other hon. members. As for me, I will not limit myself to condemning a measure that may be too weak; I say the basic principles of this bill are not bad at all.
Still, I maintain that it is not good enough to achieve the purpose of the government. To do so, we must strike at the root of the evil. The building sector must be contacted as soon as possible. The minister must hold an emergency meeting with his officials, that jointly, with the unions and manufacturers of building materials, all might sit at one table and set up concrete standards and put forward a five-year program to enable building industry to go all out and build at much lower production costs.
Thus, the government would have truly achieved something for those who have the right to own a home in this country. In addition, this would be a truly interesting investment for all Canadians.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have only three small points to make. I come from an area where on the whole we have been losing population, so that housing has not been a problem nor has serviced land been a problem. Notwithstanding the static population in two or three areas, this bill may be of value.
The first group of people who do not have adequate housing, and who will have little chance of obtaining adequate housing under existing opportunities, are the Metis and the status Indians who are moving from their traditional settlements into the towns and villages of my riding. Traditionally, these people have lived on the reservations with, generally, surrounding Metis and non-status Indian communities. There has been a rapid increase in the numbers of these people, who are finding their traditional areas are not large enough and do not provide them with the opportunities for the increased standard of living which they desire; nor is there any hope that in these areas a better standard will materialize for them.
Nearly all these people have a low level of skill. They have casual work habits and are generally ill-equipped to carry on in a modern urban centre or even at the village level. Many have large families, and a good many are totally or partially on welfare. Home owners, and there are a few sort of professional rental entrepreneurs in these villages and towns, are reluctant to rent in many cases because of fear that damage will occur to the rented property, and sometimes this does occur. Housing for these people is slow to materialize because, even under the best circumstances, rental returns are low. Yet I believe that in the long run the movement of these people from their rural ghettos to areas where there are more job opportunities will be the only way in which they have a better chance of achieving material progress. In this area there certainly will have to be substantial government assistance for this desirable event to occur, even in the short run of a decade or so, before an impact is made on this problem. I look forward to seeing how the legislation will assist villages and towns to cope with this problem.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a word or two about the low-rental housing projects that have been carried on in my area under the aegis of the provincial government. It is my understanding that 75 per cent of the funds going into low-rental housing is supplied by the federal government. In the beginning it was largely assumed that local housing committees, consisting of interested citizens, would have a large input into the locations, housing standards, etc. Perhaps some towns have functioned better than others, but certainly some towns are showing severe disillusionment with their role. The general feeling is that the towns are largely bypassed by officialdom from the city of Winnipeg and that the input at the local level is seriously reduced.
The idea of a local housing committee seems to be a good one, if it would function properly. It is obvious that even with highly trained experts and information a particular village or town will make serious mistakes. I have noticed that low-rental housing in my town are not in keeping with other houses in the area in which they are situated, although the houses themselves, as far as I know, are reasonably adequate. I believe that the federal government, having so much financial input in these building
National Housing Act
projects, should be aware of the disillusionment of the local housing committees and should take steps to rectify the situation.
Mr. Speaker, there is a group of house owners who, so far as I can see from the minister's speech, will not benefit from this bill. I refer to the so-called mobile home owners. There are hundreds of thousands of Canadians who fall into this category and who apparently receive no assistance for housing in the form of loans, etc., available to other Canadians. Yet many of these people are the ones working at unpleasant jobs, living on our frontiers and opening up new parts of our country. There are many who live, of necessity, in small communities for a time. All these people in many ways deserve more facilities for mortgages, loans, etc., than their more permanently situated Canadian friends. After all, the present housing act has a considerable element of subsidy about it. It seems likely that the use of mobile and movable homes in small communities will expand in the future. Certainly, they seem especially logical for use in our northern communities. This bill, seemingly, has done nothing for home owners in this category.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank the House for the time allotted to me.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING NEIGHBOURHOOD IMPROVEMENT, REHABILITATION, OWNERSHIP, NEW COMMUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to say a few words on such an important bill. I wanted to say these few words, because this bill is extremely important and deals with one of the prime factors of our economy.
As the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) has said, we are faced with a basic economic problem and we have to solve it. This bill is far from providing the proper solutions we need to deal with the housing problem.
Mr. Speaker, the National Housing Act is pinning people by the throat; citizens see their names used as security by financial institutions. This is where we stand now, Mr. Speaker.
Homeowners are in a position to realize this. Some 25-, 50- or 100-year old buildings are still mortgaged for more than their actual value; they are so heavily mortgaged that their owners can no longer afford to have them repaired. This is our present situation, Mr. Speaker.
I would now like to elaborate on the human aspect of housing and the right of ownership. Man has requirements that have to be met and he requires a certain degree of freedom to be truly the master of his destiny.
Private property, Mr. Speaker, is one of the most vital needs of man. Every citizen should own a home, a garden, furniture, a regular supply of consumer goods, his car, the tools of his trade, etc. It is man's personal property that enables him to settle on a parcel of land which belongs to him and to organize his own activities as well as those of his family. It is through property that he lives in unison with the physical universe.
Mr. Speaker, if life is a journey, man must be able to come to port as often as his activities permit him to do so. That port must be his own.

March 22, 1973
National Housing Act
Today, Mr. Speaker, what should be every citizen's harbour is owned by somebody else, because houses are over-mortgaged. The loans granted for 40 years to allow individuals to have a house, tend to get them into a 40-year debt and are far from making homeowners of them.
It is then, Mr. Speaker, that a citizen stops and "recharges his physical and moral batteries" and plans for tomorrow if he owns his house. Man can only come to fulfilment if he is deep-rooted in a land of his own which he can use as he sees fit. But man must also be deep-rooted in society.
Mr. Speaker, a citizen who owns a piece of land, who owns a small house, is very much interested in the administration of his municipality, his province and his country. But if he does not own anything at all, how could he be interested? On the other hand, there is no problem for the man who works alone, who has a property, a trade and enjoys the result of his work.
Mr. Speaker, if ownership is a good thing and a true need of man, and if furthermore it is a guarantee of freedom and independence, why take it from the individual to transfer it to a state which will abuse it. The answer is to ensure ownership to everyone without however taking anything away from anyone.
This is where the principles of-Social Credit can come into effect. But I will not say more on this matter, for I think I have already said enough. Personal interest is and remains the most powerful motive for human activity. As long as it is limited to a small number of individuals, and condemns the great majority of the others to work, without interest, it becomes absurd and perpetuates a society of masters and slaves and not a well structured society of men.
I have much to say on this subject, but as it is late, I will limit myself to those further comments. I should like to say a few words about the measures we could take to give our citizens the means to get at least the necessities, that is a suitable roof, under normal conditions. Now, we cannot do it today because Canadians are too poor. Why are they so poor? Why do they go without houses of their own? It is so because they were dispossessed by this despicable system under which interest rates are too high. And as a solution, they should be reduced and money should be made available to all Canadians because housing is a basic need.
All this, Mr. Speaker, should be financed at administrative cost. That is what we are asking for, what we could do and, in this way, we could give all Canadians what they are entitled to. Taxes and interest rates should be lowered; municipal taxes and property taxes should be deductible for income tax purposes.
Presently the II per cent federal sales tax on building material as well as the 8 per cent provincial tax-that turns out to be 19 per cent-are applicable on property at the expense of those who want to build a house.
Mr. Speaker, this is prohibitive and we should fight to death against these odious taxes which boost the cost of houses and prevent citizens from possessing what they are entitled to.
People are discouraged by the repayment period. It is cruel to require someone to go into debt for 40 years in order to be able to live in his own house with his family.
Anyone wishing to build a house should be able to pay it over ten years at the most; 20 years, 30 years, 40 years is much too long. People get discouraged. Moreover, the cost of houses is too high.
In view of the present state of technology, the government should ask experts to find other means of building houses at a lesser cost and with cheaper building methods, because there is surely something to be done in the building area. Our building methods are old-fashioned. They are too costly and increase the building costs. We should, therefore, find other methods.
I ask the minister to intervene and to try and convince the government to assign researchers exclusively to the field of housing; so that they may find real solutions, adequate building methods which would result in lower building costs; building costs must be reduced by at least 50 per cent.
If we are to find ways of building houses at reasonable prices, something will certainly have to be done, and we know that there is something to be done at this time.
I listed a few sectors in which we could bring about reductions in building costs, promote research in order to find ways of building cheaply, thus enabling all those who wish to become home owners to do so, because if we really want to have strong, determined and honest citizens, they must own something.
If we want to bind our citizens to our country, to have them love this country, we must create the necessary ties. To bring them closer to their country, we must see to it that they own something, so that they may settle on a piece of land belonging to them and say that that small piece of land is their own. They must also be in a position to become more ambitious citizens, the pride of this country.
I still have many things to say, but as it is getting late, I shall be satisfied with these few remarks.

subtopic: OIL-WRECK OF THE "IRVING WHALE"-POSSIBLE SOURCE OF POLLUTION
OIL-WRECK OF THE "IRVING WHALE"-POSSIBLE SOURCE OF POLLUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry to keep this House late; on the other hand, it is not my fault that we are running over our time. On February 28, in answer to a written question regarding the raising of the Irving Whale, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) advised me that the data which he had on hand favoured the leaving of the barge at the bottom of the Gulf of St. Lawrence. The minister also indicated that tenders had been received for the raising of the ship or relieving it of its cargo. The estimates ranged from $1,770,000 to $4,400,000. The minister indicated that the tenders were much higher than estimated. He also went on to point out that there was no guarantee that there would be no risk of pollution as a result of the methods of salvage submitted.
I found the answer disappointing, disheartening and disturbing, Mr. Speaker. We are in this country becoming belatedly more and more conscious of the grave danger to our ecology from massive pollution. We hear daily about the very legitimate anxieties of the people of British Columbia as consideration is given to the transfer of great quantities of oil from Alaska down to other parts of the United States. I share the anxiety of these people and I am frustrated by the government's lack of leadership in this regard. But pollution in any part of the country is important, and the threat that the Irving Whale holds for the people of Prince Edward Island and the other Atlantic provinces is real; it is serious; it is important. I cannot rest content until either the ship or its cargo is taken out of there and our beaches, our fisheries, our tourist industry, our wildfowl are relieved of this constant hazard of the escaping of oil from the hull of that ship.
One thing in the minister's answer which shocked me was the revelation that since 1971 the only kind of inspection made of the hull of the Irving Whale was on the water surface or from aircraft. In other words, no divers have been sent down to examine the state of the ship, to examine the dangers of seepage of serious quantities of oil. Surely a most careful check should be made on the hull of the craft.
The minister in his written reply indicated that there was no guarantee that the tenderers would be able to remove the ship or its cargo without the danger of pollution, and of course I accept this statement. But I also heard from the minister a few days later, in reply to an oral question, that there was in fact no guarantee against pollution if the ship were left where it is. I cannot believe that in our stage of advanced technology it is impossible for the government of Canada, with all its expertise, to handle the job of getting the cargo out of the Irving Whale. If another land can place men on the moon; if our modern science can place instruments precisely on planets, surely to haaven the raising of this ship safely is not

March 22, 1973
Adjournment Debate
beyond our technical competence and our scientific knowledge. I believe the ship can be raised.
I believe there is a good deal of importance attached to the second portion of the minister's reply, namely, the cost. I regret that the cost is so high that it could go up to $4 million. I cannot tell whether these are realistic costs, but I would have to say to the minister and his estimable parliamentary secretary that they must think also of the enormous cost which Prince Edward Island and the Atlantic community would have to pay if there should be, as a result of the ship being left there, an ecolo-catastrophe.
I think of what it would do to our fishing industry, our tourist industry and to the general well-being of our people. I say that an amount of $4 million is not toe high a price to pay. I strongly urge the minister to renew his efforts to upgrade his priorities and to call upon the very best minds, the best scientists, the best technicians and to spend money if necessary to the end that this threat which has been hanging over us for so long, since 1970, will be removed.
I cannot rest content while the Irving Whale is sitting at the bottom of the Gulf of St. Lawrence. We know what happens to ships' hulks. I understand that the Norwegians are raising the great battleship Von Tirpitz because they are afraid of pollution. We live in an age when it is now considered technically feasible to go down to get the Titanic. That would be a "Titanic" undertaking. Surely the task is not too great so far as the Gulf of St. Lawrence is concerned. I can tell the minister he need not be sensitive about the cost. Surely no member of the House of Commons or no thoughtful Canadian could begrudge the expenditure of some millions of dollars if it protected the environment of my province and the neighbouring provinces. We talk about being environment conscious. I say that the Irving Whale is a good case in point where we can prove our sincerity in this field. I urge and I plead, I persuade, I enjoin, I implore the minister to move on the matter to move the Irving Whale, and do it safely and just as soon as humanly and technically possible.

subtopic: OIL-WRECK OF THE "IRVING WHALE"-POSSIBLE SOURCE OF POLLUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to assure the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) that I shall convey to the minister the message he has given us tonight in such stirring fashion. I think, after the minister reads this particular speech which has been made on behalf of the hon. member's constituents and the people in the area concerned, he may respond in a manner satisfactory to the hon. member.
However, in respect of the answer to the question asked by the hon. member on March 5, I should like to say that there is no guarantee that marine pollution will not take place if the Irving Whale is left where it is. Numerous inquiries in areas of expertise on oil biodegradation and steel corrosion in the environment indicate that where the Irving Whale is, there is little information in respect of the oil which exists. However, it is suggested that the vessel would be safer from a pollution point of view if it were left where it is. It has also been suggested by salvage experts that there is a better than 50 per cent chance, 
unless conditions are perfect, that the vessel could break up during the removal process, causing a severe pollution problem.

subtopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-ACTIVITIES OF PROFESSIONAL DREE COUNSELLORS-GOVERNMENT ACTION
REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-ACTIVITIES OF PROFESSIONAL DREE COUNSELLORS-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are many aspects of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion that are of great importance and that concern me a great deal. One of the issues which came to my attention some time ago, and which I brought to the attention of the minister, concerns the practice of professional DREE consultants which appears to me at least as objectionable. I brought this to the minister's attention on February 2. In fact, I asked him two questions that day, one having to do with the apparent confusion, the allegations by a company in Montreal called Alarme de Surete Inc., that DREE procedures involved them in unnecessary expense and ultimately involved them in litigation.
Subsequent to that I asked the minister about this business of DREE consultants. He replied that he did not see anything different between engaging a consultant of this type and engaging a member of the legal profession to carry on some type of counselling service. I say to the minister and to the House that there is a great difference between acting as a legal counsellor and acting as a consultant if, when acting as a consultant one is acting as a lobbyist or, to put it unkindly, as a fixer. I do not know the extent of what may be the activities of these DREE consultants, but it is a very intriguing subject and it seems to be spreading to other departments.
I see that my colleague from the NDP, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby, (Mr. Broadbent), today dealt with the same sort of thing when t}e asked questions concerning the activities of the former minister of industry, trade and commerce, Mr. Jean-Luc Pepin. In today's Montreal Gazette there are some interesting quotes and references, one of which is that Mr. Pepin does not deny he is taking advantage of his past experience as minister. Part of his staff are former government officials but they would have left the public service anyway, said Mr. Pepin. I do not wish to cast aspersions on the character of this former minister. He was one of my favourite ministers in the House-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
subtopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-ACTIVITIES OF PROFESSIONAL DREE COUNSELLORS-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext: And mine also.

subtopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-ACTIVITIES OF PROFESSIONAL DREE COUNSELLORS-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
-and I am sure that he intends nothing wrong in what he is doing, any more perhaps than these consultants intend anything wrong. It is not generally known, but for the record let me say that there are several of these firms functioning in a so-called advisory capacity, mostly in urban centres. There is a prominent firm called Major and Martin which operates from 1440 St. Catherine Street West in Montreal. Here in Ottawa there is a prominent firm celled Cam Ure which operates from 2827 Riverside Drive. There is another, a former employee of the Prince Edward Island government, who acts as a DREE consultant.
March 22, 1973

The need to know your way around government red tape in order to ensure a favourable and quick grant no doubt has prompted these men to leave the government service and set up counselling firms, and also the apparent constipation of DREE at the decision-making level provides a continuous supply of frustrated clients for these people.
This, to my mind, is a fairly serious situation. Surely DREE, with its many hundreds of employees, has people who are qualified and whose duty it should be to take frustrated people in tow and to help them in their search for legitimate assistance from the department and so avoid the trouble and expense that these taxpayers, these would-be industrialists or would be entrepreneurs are encountering.
To the best of my information, the cost to people who are so frustrated that they must resort to consultants is considerable. According to my information, a retainer is charged and perhaps as much as 10 per cent of the grant obtained, or some other fixed charge is made to cover operating expenses and possible loss if they are not successful in getting a grant. Again, I suggest that probably 20 per cent of the total number of applicants are using counselling services. I suggest that is a reasonable estimate and it amounts to a considerable number of people. I would like to know the percentage of applications accepted of those people who are using these consultants, as opposed to those who are "going it" on their own.
Another thing that I do not like to see is a situation which I know sounds ridiculous. The next thing we know is that these firms are continuing to prosper. They apparently are over their frustration and have solved the problems of applicants, and the next thing we will find is that they have applied for a DREE grant themselves. This is a sort of reductio ad absurdum, but the way things have been going it would not surprise me.
I would hope that when the committee meets in the near future, the minister or some of his officials will be prepared to bring an estimate before us of just how widespread this practice has become. I hope they will give us the necessary information and, hopefully, will be able to assure us that the administrative processes have been improved to the point where this kind of nefarious service for applicants is no longer necessary and, according to their best information, has been stamped out as far as possible.

The minister in his reply on February 2 made it very clear to the hon. member that such assistance is available from his officials and, if any changes are required to make it more effective, that he is willing to make these changes. It is important to note, however, that while the
Adjournment Debate
basic responsibility for preparing information required for the analysis of a proposal must rest with the applicant, companies applying for DREE incentive grants have access to various departmental officials who are willing to explain the program at length. Industrial development officers working in Ottawa and the regions are prepared to counsel prospective applicants to make them aware of the various details and benefits under RDIA.
The hon. member also referred to-I quote from his question of February 2-"professional DREE counsellors who are making substantial profits acting on behalf of DREE applicants." The department is aware that several consultants were formerly employed by DREE, but there is certainly no evidence of any breach of the Official Secrets Act respecting the use of confidential information, or any preferred treatment.

Jean-Luc Pepin. Even though what I am about to say may not be part of the answer to his question, I am sure the hon. gentleman will be interested in it, Mr. Speaker. I was just reading a few notes on this subject, and may I say that if we consider it wise, not only for DREE but as a general principle for all other departments, for an officer who will be evaluating a proposal not to be too closely involved in its preparation, I think this could be the subject of future useful discussion and debate.

subtopic: MANPOWER-LOCAL INITIATIVES PROGRAM-INQUIRY RESPECTING GRANT TO "CENTRE EPIC", MONTREAL
MANPOWER-LOCAL INITIATIVES PROGRAM-INQUIRY RESPECTING GRANT TO "CENTRE EPIC", MONTREAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, because of the lateness of the hour I will try to be as brief as possible and to speak as quickly as I can. Yesterday I put a question to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) about the granting of $128,000 under the Local Initiatives Program to a group of Montreal businessmen, allegedly to start a health centre called Centre Epic, to fight the unhealthy effects of overdrinking, oversmoking and underexercising. I asked the minister if he would consider rescinding that grant, and whether he would list all applications that were turned down in Montreal, because this group of wealthy businessmen had received this grant of $128,000.
The question is whether a government program such as LIP should have funds going out to wealthy business groups, or whether they should be earmarked for those disadvantaged people in society, community groups or other people who need them, need jobs and need to better themselves in our society. I noted that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) said in Montreal that grants for local initiatives programs are for the

March 22, 1973
Adjournment Debate
advantaged as well as the disadvantaged groups in our society, according to an article in one of the newspapers.
This group, Centre Epic-"etude pilote en collaboration avec 1'Institut de Cardiologie"-in Montreal received a $128,000 grant. Mr. Speaker, the group was set up in 1968. I notice that on the board of directors we have such distinguished businessmen as Philipe de Gaspe Beaubien, president of Telemedia and Sport Participation Canada; Jean Boulanger, general manager of Banque Canadienne Nationale; Robert Dulude, lawyer and secretary of Mont-real-Matin; Pierre Shooner, general manager of the Montreal Chambre de Commerce; and Maurice Bigras, assistant general manager of the Provincial Bank of Canada.
I also understand that about 170 members of this centre have donated $1,000 apiece to get it going. The facilities are open to members only, and the membership fee for the health club is $150 a year. The facilities include a swimming pool, sauna, two gymnasiums, physiotherapy room, track, and equipment room which are at the disposal of the members.
Mr. Speaker, I understand that the Minister of Manpower and Immigration said this centre would benefit more than just the members; it would benefit 10,000 or 15,000 people in the Montreal area. I understand that the yearly dues are $150. It will provide assistance, through health evaluation courses, for health evaluation reports. Again I go to the article in the Montreal Gazette. I find there that use of the health centre facilities will be restricted to dues-paying members, although health evaluations made with federal studies and computers will be available to any Montrealer referred to the centre by a medical doctor. They are not saying they can use the facilities; they are saying they have access to health evaluation reports. I wonder how much health that will bring to many ordinary citizens of Montreal.
Because of the lateness of the hour I would ask the parliamentary secretary to reply to my question, particularly on the point of whether we should be disbursing
revenue for a program like this to a group in the city of Montreal, or anywhere, that is made up of business people who are millionaires or presidents of companies.

speakeroldname: Mr. Mark MacGuigan (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
subtopic: MANPOWER-LOCAL INITIATIVES PROGRAM-INQUIRY RESPECTING GRANT TO "CENTRE EPIC", MONTREAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what the LIP criteria require is that persons employed on LIP projects' be unemployed and seeking work prior to their being hired. Consequently, the organization, individual or municipality managing a project may be affluent, which is often the case in many large and reputable charitable organizations. Those who are employed on this project and creating the centre are people who were previously unemployed.
Centre Epic, which is derived from the French term for the Heart Institute Pilot Study, has received provincial concurrence and support of members of the Institute of Cardiology in Montreal. It was assessed and approved as meeting all the criteria of LIP programs, and will create 1,095 man-weeks of employment for those unemployed in construction trades. It will also provide a centre for preventive medicine dealing specifically with cardiac problems in collaboration with the Montreal Institute of Cardiology.
It will provide for recreational and medical research facilities in co-operation with the Montreal Institute of Cardiology and is going to be operated, as I understand it, as a non-profit foundation for the benefit of many Montrealers. Actually, the facilities of the club, which has some 200 members, are being built on a scale to accommodate
4,000	persons. In sum, the program aims both at the creation of jobs and at community benefit, and we think that on both these scores it has rightly been given a LIP grant.
